Isomerization: The dihydroxyacetone 3-phosphate is ultimately changed into its isomer, the glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (G3P). In this way preparatory phase is completed. Next phase of glycolysis is proceeded by two molecules of G3P, therefore, the remaining reactions occur twice. Dehydrogenation and Phosphorylation: Each G3P is oxidized by NAD and at the same time phosphorylated by inorganic phosphate (Pi) to form 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate. Substrate Level Phosphorylation: In this step a molecule of ATP is produced by substrate level phosphorylation. 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate loses its phosphate group to ADP forming ATP and is changed into 3-phosphoglycerate. Isomerization: In this step position of phosphate group is changed from C3 to C2. 3-phosphoglycerate is converted to 2-phosphoglycerate. Glycolysis is also called Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas pathway. Dehydration: In this step, 2-phosphoglycerate loses a water molecule and is converted into phosphoenol pyruvate.

Formation of ATP: Again a molecule of ATP is produced by substrate level phosphorylation when phosphoenol pyruvate loses its phosphate group which is taken up by ADP to form ATP in the presence of an enzyme (pyruvate kinase). The phosphoenol pyruvate is finally converted into pyruvate. 4 Oxidation of Pyruvate Pyruvates are produced in cytosol. Because pyruvate is a charged molecule, it must enter the mitochondrion via active transport with the help of a transport protein. On entering the mitochondria, pyruvates do not directly participate in Krebs cycle but they undergo an intermediate phase, called oxidation of pyruvate or link reaction as a part of aerobic respiration before entering into Krebs cycle. This reaction occurs in the mitochondrial matrix. Each pyruvate molecule undergoes oxidation. First, it undergoes decarboxylation, in which a molecule of CO2 is removed from pyruvate to form a two-carbon compound called acetyl group. Then, NAD removes hydrogen atoms (oxidation) from the acetyl group to produce acetyl-CoA and NADH. Acetyl-CoA now enters the Krebs cycle. 5 Krebs Cycle This cycle was discovered by German scientist Sir Hans Krebs, therefore, called Krebs cycle. It is also called citric acid cycle or Tri carboxylic acid (TCA) cycle because the first compound which is formed in the cycle is citrate (citric acid) that contains three carboxylic acid groups. The Krebs cycle comprises following nine steps: Synthesis Acetyl CoA (2-carbon compound) and a water molecule combine with oxaloacetate (4-carbon compound) to form a 6-carbon compound called citrate (citric acid). It is the first product of Krebs cycle. CoA is liberated. Dehydration Citrate undergoes reorganization by the removal of a water molecule. The resulting compound is cis-aconitate. Hydration Cis-aconitate is converted into isocitrate with the addition of water. Actually, citrate and isocitrate are isomers of each other. Oxidative decarboxylation This is a two-step process, which involves oxidation/dehydrogenation of isocitrate, followed by the decarboxylation to form alpha-ketoglutarate. The hydrogen and electrons which are released from isocitrate are taken up by NAD to form NADH while the carboxyl group is released in the form of CO2. Oxidative decarboxylation and addition of CoA Alpha-ketoglutarate again undergoes oxidative decarboxylation. The hydrogen and electrons which are released from alpha-ketoglutarate are taken up by NAD to form NADH and the carboxyl group is released in the form of CO2. Then, it combines with coenzyme A forming succinyl CoA. Formation of ATP CoA is removed from Succinyl CoA to form succinate. The reaction releases energy which is used to combine GDP and Pi forming GTP. GTP reacts with ADP to form ATP and GDP is again converted into GDP. In this way a molecule of ATP is produced. Dehydrogenation/oxidation Succinate undergoes dehydrogenation/oxidation to form fumarate. The hydrogen and electrons which are released from succinate are taken up by FAD to form FADH2. Hydration A water molecule gets added to fumarate to form malate. Oxidation Malate undergoes dehydrogenation/oxidation to produce oxaloacetate. The hydrogen and electrons which are released from malate are taken up by NAD to form NADH.

Oxaloacetate picks up another molecule of acetyl CoA to repeat the cycle. 6 Electron Transport Chain (ETC) Most of the energy of glucose is in the form of NADH and FADH2. Their energy is released through Electron Transport Chain. In this chain, the reduced coenzymes are oxidized and the electrons are passed along a series of oxidation-reduction reactions. The components of electron transport chain include: (1) NADH-dehydrogenase complex (I), (2) FADH-dehydrogenase complex (II), (3) coenzyme Q, (4) Cytochrome reductase complex (III), (5) Cytochrome c, (6) Cytochrome oxidase complex (IV). Sequence of electron flow NADH is oxidized when it reacts with NADH-dehydrogenase complex (I). The electrons now move to the mobile carrier co-enzyme Q. If FADH2 is to be oxidized through ETC, it also transfers its electrons to coenzyme Q, via FADH dehydrogenase complex (II). The flowing electrons from coenzyme Q are now transferred to cytochrome reductase complex (III) which hands over its electron to cytochrome c. Like co-enzyme Q, cytochrome c is also mobile carrier of electrons. Cytochrome c delivers the electrons to cytochrome oxidase complex (IV). Finally, the electrons are transferred to oxygen. Each oxygen atom becomes reactive. It also picks up a pair of hydrogen ions from the aqueous solution forming water. During the passage of electrons from one carrier to next, energy is released. Part of this energy is used to pump protons (H) from the mitochondrial matrix into the inter-membrane space. There are three such sites, corresponding to three complexes in the electron transport chain i.e. NADH-dehydrogenase complex (I), cytochrome reductase complex (III) and cytochrome oxidase complex (IV). MDCATBYFUTUREDOCTORS(TOUSEEFAHMADKHAN) 03499815886 How does the electron transport chain make ATP? The coupling of electron transport chain and ATP synthesis is called chemiosmosis. Chemiosmosis and Oxidative Phosphorylation Oxidative phosphorylation is the synthesis of ATP molecules with the help of energy released during oxidation of reduced co-enzymes (NADH, FADH2) produced in respiration. The enzyme required for this synthesis is called ATP synthase. ATP synthase is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane. It consists of two parts i.e., Fo and F1. Fo is embedded in the membrane and involves in the movement of protons from inter-membrane space to mitochondrial matrix. F1 or head particle is attached to the surface of membrane towards matrix. It catalyzes ATP synthesis by combining ADP and Pi. ATP-synthase becomes active in ATP synthesis when a proton gradient having higher concentration of protons on the inter-membrane side is established. The flow of protons down their concentration gradient through the Fo channel provides energy that is used by ATP-synthase to produce ATP. This produces ATP. Oxidative phosphorylation produces about 32 ATP molecules while a similar mechanism during light reaction produces ATP in chloroplasts. 7 Substrate Level Phosphorylation The prime objective of cellular respiration is to generate ATPs. There are two ways to do this during aerobic respiration: chemiosmosis and substrate level phosphorylation, however we have already discussed.

As far as substrate level phosphorylation is concerned, you are already familiar that addition of inorganic phosphate to any organic molecule is called phosphorylation. Thus, when phosphate is enzymatically transferred from an organic substrates molecule it is called substrate level phosphorylation. However, it accounts for only a small percentage of the ATP that a cell generates. It occurs at three occasions during aerobic respiration. In glycolysis, substrate level phosphorylation occurs when 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate is converted to 3-phosphoglycerate (7th reaction) and when phosphoenol pyruvate is converted to pyruvate (10th reaction). There are four ATPs produced by this mechanism but two of them are supposed to be consumed in preparatory phase of glycolysis. So net ATP produced by substrate level phosphorylation is 2 ATP. In Krebs cycle, substrate level phosphorylation occurs when succinyl CoA is converted to succinate. There are two molecules of ATP produced at this occasion. Since, ATP can be synthesized directly from the organic substrates of exergonic reactions (energy releasing reactions e.g., cellular respiration), therefore, it is said that substrate level phosphorylation couples the exergonic reactions with the synthesis of ATP. These ATPs are used to drive endergonic reactions (energy storing reaction e.g., protein synthesis). In this way, out of total 36 ATP which are produced during aerobic respiration in human cells, 4 ATP are the result of substrate level phosphorylation and the remaining 32 ATP are produced by chemiosmosis through electron transport chain. 8 Importance of G3P Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (G3P) is an important intermediate of respiration and photosynthesis. In respiration, G3P appears during glycolysis pathway which leads to the formation of pyruvate. In the Calvin cycle of photosynthesis, G3P molecules are converted to glucose phosphate within the chloroplast. Glucose phosphate is then converted to glucose, fructose, sucrose and starch. 9 Respiration of Fats and Proteins When fat is used as an energy source, it breaks down to glycerol and three fatty acids. Glycerol is converted to G3P, a metabolite in glycolysis. Fatty acids are converted to acetyl-CoA, which enters the Krebs cycle. An 18-carbon fatty acid results in nine acetyl-CoA molecules. Breakdown of proteins results in amino acids whose R-group size determines whether the carbon chain is oxidized in glycolysis or the Krebs cycle. The carbon chain is oxidized when an amino acid undergoes deamination, i.e., the removal of the amino group. The amino group becomes ammonia (NH3), which enters the urea cycle and becomes part of urea. 3 PHOTORESPIRATION The respiratory activity that occurs in green cells in the presence of light resulting in the release of carbon dioxide is termed as photorespiration. It needs oxygen and produce CO2 and H2O like aerobic respiration. However ATP is not produced during photorespiration. 1 Mechanism of Photorespiration When the CO2 levels inside the leaf drop to around 50 ppm (part per million), ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (RuBisCO) starts to combine O2 with RuBP instead of CO2.

The net result of this is that instead of producing two 3C molecules of phosphoglycerate (PGA), only one molecule of PGA and a toxic 2C molecule called phosphoglycolate are produced. The plant must get rid of the phosphoglycolate. First it immediately gets rid of the phosphate group, converting the molecule to glycolate. Phosphoglycolate Phosphoglycerate Glycolate The glycolate is then transported to the peroxisome and a series of reactions convert it to glycine. The glycine is then transported to the mitochondria where it is converted into serine. The serine is then used to make other organic molecules. 2 Effect of temperature on the oxidative activity of RuBisCO Photorespiration is related to the functioning of the enzyme ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase. It is often called RuBisCO because it can have an oxygenase activity in addition to carboxylase activity. Its activity depends upon the relative concentration of O2 and CO2 in leaves. Photorespiration starts when the CO2 levels inside the leaf become low. This happens on hot dry days when plant begins to secrete abscisic acid which causes closing of stomata to prevent excess water loss. If the plant continues to fix CO2 in photosynthesis when its stomata are closed, the CO2 will be used up and the O2 produced from photosynthesis will be prevented to release out of plant body. In this way the O2 level in the leaf will increase relative to CO2 concentrations. 3 Cost and Evolution of Photorespiration Photorespiration costs the plant energy and results in the net loss of fixed carbon from the carbohydrate during photosynthesis. Since photorespiration is not essential for plant then why it exists? If photorespiration is inhibited chemically, the plant grows normally. Moreover there are plants which naturally resistant to photorespiration. The reason is that the active site of RuBisCO can bind both carbon dioxide and oxygen. There was no oxygen in the atmosphere at the time of establishment of photosynthesis, so the carboxylase binding activity was the only one used. The photorespiration started when the oxygen began to accumulate in the atmosphere. 4 Significance of C4 Photosynthesis: An adaptation to the problem of photorespiration Plants in hot climate have evolved an adaptation to the problem of photorespiration by developing an additional metabolic pathway in light independent phase of photosynthesis. This metabolic pathway is called Hatch-Slack cycle or C4 pathway. In this pathway the first product of CO2 fixation is a 4-carbon compound oxaloacetate, so these plants are called C4 plants e.g., maize, sugarcane, sorghum, etc. Oxaloacetate is then transported to the bundle sheath cells of mesophyll. It is then reduced to another 4-C compound, malate with the help of NADH, produced in photochemical phase. The malate is transported to the chloroplasts of bundle sheath cells. Here malate is converted to pyruvate (C3) with the release of CO2. Thus concentration of CO2 increases in the bundle sheath cells. These cells contain enzymes of Calvin cycle. Because of high concentration of CO2, RuBisCO participates in Calvin cycle and not in photorespiration.
Sugar produced in Calvin cycle is transported into the phloem. Pyruvate generated in the bundle sheath cells re-enters mesophyll cells and regenerates phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP) by consuming one ATP.

Diversity among animals INVERTEBRATES Animals are diverse in structure. There are the vast differences in structural complexity of animals from the simplest sponges to humans. Invertebrates: The animal species that lack a backbone are commonly known as invertebrates. They account for 95 of known animal species. The invertebrates have been divided into following phyla: porifera, cnidaria, platyhelminthes, aschelminthes, mollusca, annelida, arthropoda and echinodermata. Phylum Porifera (pore bearer) General characteristics of phylum porifera: Sponges are sessile, attached but their larvae are motile. Sponges are all aquatic, mostly marine, a few live in freshwater. Their size varies from a few millimetre wide to more than a metre tall. They have cellular level of organization and not organized as tissue or organs. Body lacks symmetry. The body wall consists of outer dermal layer called pinacoderm, and inner layer choanoderm made up of flagellated cells called choanocytes. The middle region is called mesenchyme. Body is perforated by many pores called ostia. There is a single cavity inside the body called spongocoel. Water enters through ostia travels through the canal and goes out by a large terminal opening called osculum. Sponges depend on food coming along with water currents. Various shapes of spicules form the skeleton. These are needle like and may be calcareous or siliceous. The bath sponge has spongin fibre. Asexual reproduction takes place by budding or gemmules. Buds develop into new sponges. Sexual reproduction takes place by egg and sperm. Sexes may be separate or hermaphrodite. The embryo development includes free swimming ciliated larval stages. Sponges have remarkable ability of regeneration from a small fragment. Sponges have evolved from the protists called choanoflagellates. The examples of sponges are: Spongilla, Sycon, etc. Evolutionary adaptations in sponges: (1) Digestion: It is completely intracellular i.e., food vacuoles within the cell. (2) Transportation: It occurs by water current system. (3) Respiration and Excretion: It takes place through diffusion. (4) Excretion: It takes place through water current. (5) Nervous system: A sponge lacks nervous system. There is an ability to coordinate the flow of water. Sponges seem to have only response to chemical stimuli. Importance of sponges: Skeleton of sponges are used for washing and bathing because of great capacity to absorb water. They are used in surgical operations for soaking fluids and blood. Sponges are used for sound absorption in buildings. Phylum Cnidaria (stinging celled organisms) General characteristics of phylum cnidaria: Cnidarians are entirely aquatic, mostly marine, few found in freshwater, e.g., Hydra. Most of the species are sessile, e.g., Hydra, others are free living and motile e.g., Jelly fish. Some are colonial e.g., Obelia. They range in size from microscopic (Hydra) to two metres in length (jelly fish). Body symmetry: radial symmetry. Cnidarians are diploblastic animals having ectoderm, endoderm and mesoglea in between the two. They have a sac like internal gastrovascular cavity, which has only one opening the mouth. The mouth is often surrounded by tentacles. Tentacles and body is provided with stinging cell organelles called nematocysts.

Asexual reproduction takes place by budding and sexual reproduction by gametes. Cnidarians also occur in the form of colonies. The units of the colonies are called zooids. There are two main types of zooids. Polyps which are feeding zooids and Medusae are reproductive zooids, for sexual reproduction. Evolutionary adaptations in cnidarians: (1) Digestion: Gastrovascular cavity is often branched or divided with septa with a single opening. (2) Transportation and excretion: Takes place through diffusion. (3) Respiration and Excretion: There is no respiratory and excretory system. (4) Nervous system: Nervous system consists of nerve net and sensory organs. Importance of cnidarians: Coral reefs protect shores from erosion by water waves. Phylum Platyhelminthes (flatworms) General characteristics of phylum platyhelminthes: The flatworms are free living, predators, or parasite, e.g., Tapeworm. They are found in freshwater, marine, animal gut, damp places. Body is soft and flattened dorsoventrally. Platyhelminthes are triploblastic and exhibit bilateral symmetry. Body cavity, coelom is absent, and the spaces are filled with mesenchyme tissue. Locomotion is not significant in some flatworms. Free living forms are motile. They have ability of regeneration of the animals, e.g., Planaria. In parasitic forms locomotion is restricted. Reproduction both by asexual and sexual means, Asexual by fission, budding, fragmentation. Sexual reproduction by copulation. Hermaphrodite. The examples of flatworms are: Dugesia (Planaria), Fasciola (liver fluke), Taenia (tapeworm). Evolutionary adaptations in platyhelminthes: (1) Digestion: Digestive system is incomplete gastrovascular cavity, having only one opening to the exterior, the mouth. (2) Respiration: Respiratory system is absent. (3) Transport: Transport system is absent. (4) Excretion: Excretory system consists of two lateral canals with branches bearing flame cells (protonephridia). (5) Nervous system: Nervous system consists of a pair of anterior ganglia with longitudinal nerve cords. Importance of platyhelminthes: The parasitic species of flukes and tapeworms are very harmful to man, e.g., tapeworm, liver fluke, the blood fluke of cattle etc. Phylum Aschelminthes (roundworms) General characteristics of phylum aschelminthes: The roundworms are free living or parasitic and in soil, roots, human and animal intestine and muscles. Most roundworms are less than five cm long and many are microscopic but some parasitic roundworms are more than one metre in length. Roundworms exhibit bilateral symmetry, having three germ layers. Body is cylindrical with tapering ends. Muscular layer is not continuous. It is divided into four longitudinal bands i.e., two dorsolateral, two ventrolateral. The body cavity is pseudocoelom. Fertilization is internal. Evolutionary adaptations in aschelminthes: (1) Digestion: Digestive system is complete with mouth and anus at opposite ends. (2) Respiration: It takes place through body surface by diffusion. (3) Transport: Transport is absent, circulation through pseudocoelomic fluid. (4) Excretion: Excretory system consists of renette gland cells and excretory canals. (5) Nervous system: Nervous system consists of circum pharyngeal nerve ring connected with ganglia and longitudinal nerve cords. Importance of aschelminthes: Ascaris lumbricoides is an intestinal parasite of man. Pinworms (Enterobius vermicularis) are parasites in the human caecum, colon and appendix causing insomnia and loss of appetite.

Phylum Mollusca (soft bodied animals) General characteristics of phylum mollusca: They are free living or sessile, and live in freshwater, marine and land (in moist places). The molluscs exhibit bilateral symmetry, are triploblastic, coelomate, soft and unsegmented animals. Body is divided into head, ventral muscular foot, dorsal visceral region. The whole animal is covered in an envelope called mantle. It secretes the shell. The shell may be external (snail), internal (cuttle fish) or even absent (octopus). Mouth cavity may have a tongue like structure called radula, e.g., Cuttle fish, snail. Coelom is divided into sinuses. Sexes may be separate, e.g., Unio or united, e.g., Helix. The development takes place through trochophore larvae. The examples of molluscs are snail, slug, oyster, freshwater mussel and Octopus etc. Evolutionary adaptations in molluscs: (1) Digestion: Digestive system is complete, partly emptying into mantle cavity. (2) Respiration: Respiration through gills, under mantle or body surface. (3) Transport: Open circulatory system with heart and blood vessels. (4) Excretion: There are one or two kidneys which open into the pericardial cavity. (5) Nervous system: The nervous system consists of cerebral, pleural, pedal and visceral ganglia with nerve cord. Importance of molluscs: Shell of freshwater mussels are used in button making. They are also used for making ornaments. Some oysters make valuable pearls. Shells are used in poultry feeds. Clams, oyster, mussels are source of food in Far East, Europe, America etc. Slugs and snails are injurious in garden and cultivation. Teredo a shipworm damage wooden parts in ships. Phylum Annelida (segmented worms) General characteristics of phylum annelida: The annelids are called segmented worms. They are free living (Earthworm) or ectoparasite (leech). They are found in soil, freshwater and marine e.g., Nereis. Body is metamerically segmented. Coelom is a true coelom divided into compartments. The coelomic fluid of the adjacent chambers serves as a hydrostatic skeleton also. The body wall consists of outer circular and inner longitudinal muscles used in locomotion. The organs of locomotion are chaetae (setae) present in the body wall of Nereis. The circulatory system of the annelids is closed. Sexes are separate in some annelids, e.g., Nereis. Others are hermaphrodite e.g., earthworm. Fertilization is external or internal. The examples are Pheretima (Earthworm), Hirudinaria (leech). Evolutionary adaptations in annelids: (1) Digestion: Digestive system is complete with mouth and anus. (2) Respiration: Respiration takes place through skin. (3) Transport: Closed circulatory system with dorsal and ventral vessels. (4) Excretion: Excretion takes place through nephridia. (5) Nervous system: Central nervous system consists of nerve ring and nerve cord, which extends throughout the body. Importance of annelids: Earthworms form an important food item for many birds and fish. Earthworms help in soil improvement. Leech is an ectoparasite to man and cattle. Phylum Arthropoda (animals with jointed legs) General characteristics of phylum arthropoda: The arthropods are called joint footed animals. They are free living or parasites and are found in all types of habitat. The body is segmented. Some are worm like and others are flying insects.

Segments are modified, specialized and fused variously distinct or fused. Body is covered by chitin. It is flexible at many places to allow articulation. There are several pairs of appendages. Coelom is not present as the main body cavity. It is reduced and is called haemocoel, because it is connected with the blood vascular system. Alimentary canal has two openings, the mouth and anus. Skeleton is exoskeleton, formed chiefly of chitin. Muscles are attached to exoskeleton for locomotion. Sexes are separate in arthropods. The male and female arthropods are often alike. The reproductive organs and ducts are paired. The testes produce sperms and ovaries produce eggs. Fertilization is mostly internal. Development takes place through metamorphosis. Evolutionary adaptations in arthropods: (1) Digestion: Digestive system is complete. (2) Respiration: Respiratory system consists of air tubes called trachea. Spiders have book lungs. Some forms have book lungs (e.g., spiders) or air tube (trachea) for respiration. (3) Transport: Circulatory system consists of dorsal contractile heart (blood is without haemoglobin). (4) Excretion: Excretion takes place by Malpighian tubules and solid uric acid is excreted. (5) Nervous system: Nervous system is well developed. There is a brain and a ventral double nerve cord. There is a ganglion in each segment from which nerves arise. Importance of arthropods: Lobsters, crayfish and prawns are eaten as food. Many arthropods act as intermediate hosts for human parasites, e.g., Cyclops carries larvae of Guinea worm. Honey and bees wax are produced by the honeybee and silk is produced by silkworm. Insects aid in the production of fruits, seeds and vegetables by pollinating flowers. Fruit fly (Drosophila), cockroach, grasshopper are abundantly used as laboratory animals for scientific learning and research. Insects destroy field crops, fruit trees and timber. They spread diseases among human beings. Bees and wasps sting, mosquitoes, lice and fleas bite and suck blood. Scorpions and a few spiders are poisonous and sting. Phylum Echinodermata (spiny skinned animals) General characteristics of phylum echinodermata: They are free living; some are attached to the substratum. The echinoderms are exclusively marine. Most are found at the bottom along the shorelines in shallow seas. Body is covered by delicate epidermis. The echinoderms are triploblastic coelomates and exhibit radial symmetry in adult. Echinoderms have an endoskeleton consisting of spine bearing calcium rich plates. The spines, which stick out through the delicate skin, account for their name. The mouth is on the oral side and anus is on the aboral side. There is a central disc from which arms radiate. The body may be flattened like biscuit (cake urchin), star-shaped with short arm (starfish) globular (sea urchin), star-shaped with long arms (brittle star) or elongated (sea cucumber). Coelom consists of canals and spaces, and one of which forms water vascular system. Organs of locomotion are the tube feet. These are present along the arms of grooves present in the arms. Sexes are separate. The fertilization is external. The larvae as bipinnaria and brachiolaria are free swimming. The regeneration is shown by the adult and larvae.

The examples are starfish, sea cucumber, brittle star and sea urchin. Evolutionary adaptations in echinoderms: (1) Digestion: Digestive system is usually complete, axial or in ophiuroids absent. (2) Respiration: Respiration is performed by dermal branchiae, tube feet, respiratory tree e.g., sea cucumber and bursae e.g., spiny brittle star. (3) Transport: Blood vascular system is much reduced. (4) Excretion: Excretory organs are absent. (5) Nervous system: Nervous system includes a circumoral nerve ring and radial nerve cords. There is no brain. Economic importance of echinoderms: Many echinoderms are used as food. Dried skeleton of echinoderms are used as fertilizer because of their high percentage of calcium and nitrogen. Starfishes act as scavengers and thus clean seawater. They cause damage to oyster beds. The stinging sea urchins are poisonous. Phylum Hemichordata (acorn worm) Characteristics of both echinoderms and chordates and both groups are placed in deuterostome branch of animal kingdom. Hemichordates are placed near chordates because of their close relationship to chordates. Examples: Balanoglossus, Saccoglossus. General characteristics of phylum hemichordata: The hemichordates are called acorn worms. All hemichordates are marine. Some are solitary, naked and slow moving; others are sedentary. Body is soft and unsegmented and has a worm like form. Body has three distinct regions: proboscis, collar and trunk. Symmetry is bilateral and hemichordates are triploblastic. Body cavity is a true coelom. Excretory system comprises of a glomerulus situated in the proboscis and connected with blood vessels. There are no nephridia. Sexes may be separate or united. Fertilization is external. Development may include free swimming larval stage. Evolutionary adaptations in hemichordates: (1) Respiration: It occurs by gill slits connecting the pharynx with outside as in chordates. (2) Circulatory system: It includes a heart and two longitudinal vessels, a dorsal and a ventral, interconnected by sinus. Blood is colourless and without corpuscles. (3) Nervous system: It is diffuse composed of epidermal plexus of nerve cells and nerve fibres. Phylum Chordata The phylum chordata called the chordates, are the most familiar and the most widely distributed animals, showing diversity of form. Main Features of Chordates Chordates possess four basic characteristics, which are: (a) notochord (b) dorsal hollow nerve cord (c) pharyngeal slits (d) post anal tail. Notochord: The notochord is an internal, flexible, rod like structure. It is present below the dorsal hollow nerve cord and above the alimentary canal. It is present throughout or part of length of the animal. Dorsal hollow nerve cord: Central nervous system of chordates consists of a single, tubular, fluid filled, nongangliated nerve cord situated along the mid dorsal line above the notochord and outside the coelom. Pharyngeal slits: The gill slits (pharyngeal clefts) are paired perforations on the lateral sides of the anterior part of the digestive tract, leading from the pharynx to exterior. Post anal tail: It extends beyond the anus, at least in embryo, but in many adult chordates it is vestigial.

Classification of Chordates The phylum chordata has been subdivided into two groups: (a) Protochordata or Acrania in which brain is not enclosed in bony case (b) Craniata in which brain is enclosed in bony case and notochord has been replaced by vertebral column. Group Protochordata (Acrania) Phylum protochordata has been divided into two sub-phyla: (i) Subphylum urochordata, (ii) Subphylum cephalochordata. Subphylum Urochordata: The body is covered by a covering called tunic and called tunicates. On the outside are two openings, incurrent siphon which corresponds to mouth and excurrent siphon corresponds to anus. The larva has a mid-dorsal hollow nerve cord and notochord in the tail, so the group is named urochordata. In the adult, the notochord is lost. Subphylum Cephalochordata: Body is fish like. It has no head but tail is present. Notochord extends the entire length of the body. There is no organ for respiration. The example of cephalochordate is: Amphioxus. Group Craniata Group craniata has one subphylum i.e., vertebrata. Subphylum Vertebrata The characteristics that give the member of this group the names vertebrata and craniates are spinal column of vertebrae, which encloses the dorsal nerve cord, brain enclosed in a skull or cranium of the body, and a well developed head. Subphylum vertebrata is divided into two superclasses: (a) Agnatha (b) Gnathostomata. Superclass Agnatha (Jawless fishes) General characteristics of super class agnatha: It is divided into two classes: Myxini and Cephalaspidomorphi. Body slender, eel-like, and rounded with naked skin. There is no median fin in class Myxini. There are one or two median fins in class Cephalaspidomorphi. The caudal fin extends anteriorly to the cloaca. Endoskeleton is cartilaginous and the notochord is persistent. Diagnostic characteristics of super class agnatha: Buccal funnel and toothed tongue: form of jaws. There are five to sixteen gills for respiration in class Myxini, seven pairs of gills each with external gill opening in class Cephalaspidomorphi. Dorsal nerve cord with differentiated brain. No paired appendages. Superclass Gnathostomata It is divided into six classes: Chondrichthyes, Osteichthyes, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia. Class Chondrichthyes (Cartilaginous fishes) General characteristics of class chondrichthyes: Body is laterally compressed and streamlined (fusiform) shaped. Mouth is ventral. Olfactory sacs are not connected to mouth cavity. Skin is tough and covered with minute placoid scale. The pectoral and pelvic fins are paired. There are one or two dorsal fins. The caudal fin is heterocercal. Endoskeleton is cartilaginous. Digestive tract leads into the cloaca. Stomach is J shaped. The circulatory system consists of two-chambered heart. There is one atrium and one ventricle. There are five pairs of aortic arches. Respiratory system includes 5-7 pairs of gills. Swim bladder is absent. Sexes are separate. Gonads are paired. Fertilization is internal. They are oviparous or viviparous. It includes the sharks, dogfishes, rays, skates. Evolutionary adaptations in class chondrichthyes: They have streamlined body for active movement. They have tough skin, placoid scales and strong jaws for predatory life. They have well developed sensory system.

Class Osteichthyes (Bony fishes) General characteristics of class osteichthyes: Body is usually spindle-shaped and streamlined for active movement through water. Endoskeleton is partly or wholly bony. Vertebrae are amphicoelous. Pelvic girdle is often absent. Notochord persists in reduced form. Skin usually contains dermal scales embedded in the dermis. Both median and paired fins are present. Pectoral and pelvic fins are paired while dorsal fin is single. The caudal fin is homocercal. Mouth is usually terminal, i.e., anterior end often bears numerous teeth. Digestive system is well developed. Anus is present and cloaca is absent. The four pairs of gills are covered by operculum. Spiracles are mostly absent. Swim bladder is usually present with or without connection with the pharynx. Circulatory system has two chambered, having only one atrium and one ventricle. Red blood cells are oval and nucleated. Brain has ten pairs of cranial nerves. Gonads are paired. Fertilization is generally external. They are oviparous. They show parental care. They include Labeo rohita, sea horse, flying fish, globe fish, catla catla, trout, codfish and eel. Latimeria, a lobe-finned fish, is a living fossil. Evolutionary adaptations in class osteichthyes: They have streamlined body, fins for swimming. Operculum protects gills. Swim bladder provides buoyancy. Lateral line system detects vibrations. The animals which are called tetrapods have four limbs. The lobe-finned fishes of the Devonian period are ancestral to the amphibians, the first tetrapods. Animals that live on land use limbs to support the body, as air is normally less buoyant than water. Lobed-finned fishes and early amphibians also had lungs and means to respire air. Class Amphibia General characteristics of class amphibia: Body varies considerably in forms, is divisible only into head and trunk. Most have two pairs of pentadactyl limbs with 4-5 or fewer digits. Some have lost legs, e.g., Caecilians. Webbed feet often present, e.g., frogs. Skin is smooth, moist and rich in glands. It is highly vascularized. Scales are generally absent. In some glands are toxic. Chromatophore pigment cells are present in the skin. In larval stage respiration takes place by gills and in the adults by lungs and skin. Heart is three chambered with respect to atria and ventricle. Sinus venosus, truncus arteriosus are present. Double circulation takes place through the heart. Sexes are separate. Gonads are paired. Fertilization may be external or internal. Most forms are oviparous. Development takes place through metamorphosis. Amphibians are anamniotes (without amnion). Body temperature is variable, i.e., poikilothermic (ectotherms) and many forms undergo hibernation in winter. The examples of amphibians are frogs, toads, salamanders, caecilian, mud puppy etc. Evolutionary adaptations in class amphibia: Limbs for movement on solid substratum. Lungs for breathing air. Internal nares to make breathing possible by keeping mouth closed. Slimy skin for protection against desiccation. Changed in circulatory system to provide respiration by lungs and skin. There is reduction in bones to make the body lighter. Transition from Aquatic to Land Habitat Amphibians lie on the borderline between aquatic and true terrestrial animals.

The amphibian reproduction is dependent on water so the amphibians are not a successful group owing to their dependence on water for reproduction and development. Class Reptilia General characteristics of class reptilia: There are two pairs of pentadactyl limbs, typically with five digits. Skin is rough, cornified and dry, which is adapted to land life. Heart is incompletely four chambered, having two atria and partly divided ventricle. Crocodiles have completely four chambered heart. Reptiles are cold blooded animals, i.e., poikilothermic (ectotherms) and hibernate in winter. Sexes are separate. Gonads are paired. Fertilization is internal. Most forms are oviparous. Eggs are large, amniotic and have large yolk eggs. Eggs are enclosed by leathery or limy shell for protection. Embryo is protected by three embryonic membranes known as amnion, allantois and chorion. The examples of reptiles are tortoise, lizard, snake, crocodile and alligator etc. Evolutionary adaptations in class reptilia: Reptiles show the advancement over the amphibians in having: (a) A dry skin which enables them to live away from water. (b) Separation of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood in the heart. (c) A neck movable independent of the body. (d) Better mechanism of breathing. (e) Fertilization is internal. (f) Egg with shell for protection on land. Class Aves General characteristics of class aves: Body of aves is streamlined and adapted for flying. It is divided into head, neck, a trunk and a tail. Neck is very long and flexible. There are two pairs of pentadactyl limbs. The forelimbs are modified to form wings. Hind limbs are strong and adapted for perching, walking or swimming. Digits are armed with horny claws. The skin is covered by an epidermal horny covering of feathers all over the body and scales on the feet. Due to air cavities, skeleton is light. Skull has large sockets. Jaws extend into horny beak. Teeth are absent. Heart is four chambered, having two atria and two ventricles. There is only right aorta. It curves to the right side then bends backward. Birds are endothermic. Respiration takes place only by lungs. There are one pair of kidneys. The ureters open into the cloaca. In birds urine is semisolid and uric acid is main nitrogenous waste. Fertilization is internal. Eggs are large with much yolk. Only one ovary is functional. Some birds have secondarily lost the power of flight and are called flightless birds e.g., ostrich, kiwi, etc. Evolutionary adaptations in class aves: An insulated covering over the body is present. Air circulation in the lungs, taking place during both inspiration and expiration. Complete separation of venous and arterial blood in the heart. A regulated body temperature keeps the aves equally active all the year round. Patterns of behaviour, such as care for the young ones, nest building, courtship and affection for the mate and migration, which are practically unknown in reptiles. Class Mammalia General characteristics of class mammalia: Body is variously shaped and divisible into a head, a neck, a trunk and a tail. There are two pairs of pentadactyl limbs.

These are variously adapted for walking, running, burrowing and swimming or flying. Skin is glandular, mostly covered by hair. Coelom is completely divided into anterior smaller thoracic cavity and posterior larger cavity by a muscular partition the diaphragm, which is present only in the mammals. Endoskeleton is fully ossified. Skull has two occipital condyles, large cranium. External ear or pinna is present. There is a chain of three bones in the ear incus, malleus and stapes. Mammals have deciduous and permanent teeth. Heart is four chambered. Only left aortic arch is present. Red blood cells are non-nucleated. Mammals are warm blooded (endothermic) animals. Voice apparatus is well developed, and consists of larynx and epiglottis. Mammals give birth to their young ones. Mammals feed them on milk produced by mammary glands of mother. Mammals are classified into three subclasses: (1) Prototheria-Egg laying mammals. (2) Metatheria-Pouched mammals. (3) Eutheria-Placental mammals. Subclass Prototheria - The Monotremes The subclass Prototheria is a connecting link between reptiles and mammals and is evidence of evolution and origin of mammals from reptiles. Certain members of this subclass have some adaptations for aquatic life, e.g., Duck bill platypus, which has a bill similar to that of duck, and has webbed toes. The mammalian feature of the monotremes is that the young are fed on mothers milk and they feed their youngs. The reptilian features include laying of eggs, single opening for urinogenital and digestive systems called cloaca. The monotremes are found in Australia. The examples of monotremes are Duckbill platypus, spiny ant eater. Subclass Metatheria - The Marsupials The females have an abdominal pouch the marsupium, where they rear their young. The young ones when borne are immature. The nipples are in the pouch. The mother feeds the young ones and carries them in the pouch till they are matured enough. The Marsupials are found in Australia and America. The examples of Marsupials are: opossum, kangaroo and Koala. Sub-class Eutheria - The Placentals Development of young one takes place inside the body of the mother. The youngs are bore fully developed. Developing placental mammals are dependent on placenta (an organ of exchange between maternal blood and fetal blood.) So these mammals are called placental mammals. Nutrients are supplied to the growing offspring, and wastes are passed to the mother for excretion. The young ones are born at a relatively advanced stage of development. The placental mammals have maximum mammalian characteristics. In some hair may be modified into scales in pangolin, and spines in porcupine. Examples of the placental mammals are man, whale, elephant, horse, rat, mice, bat, dolphin, cat, tiger, lion, monkey, etc. Evolutionary adaptations in class mammalia: A regulated body temperature. This makes them independent of environmental change, keeping active throughout the year. Complete separation of blood in the heart. More efficient mechanism of respiration and circulation. An active life and a high rate of metabolism. A separate respiratory passage that avoids interference in breathing during feeding. Better developed senses of smell, sight and hearing.

A more highly developed nervous system. Large cerebrum and cerebellum provide for better coordination in all activities and retentive memory. Patterns of behaviour, such as care and nursing of the young ones.

Diversity among plants Diagnostic Features of Plants Plants are multicellular eukaryotes with well-developed tissue and have autotrophic nutrition. Plants are well protected from being dried up in air by their cuticle, formed from a waxy substance called cutin. The plant body has root, stems and leaves having vascular tissue xylem, phloem and cellulose rich cell walls. Plants show alternation of generation. It consists of the sporophyte the diploid generation that produces haploid spores by meiosis. Spores develop into a haploid generation. The gametophyte is the haploid generation which produces gametes that unite to form a diploid zygote. The gametes are eggs and sperms. NON-VASCULAR PLANTS Plants are currently divided into two main groups: the nonvascular or bryophytes, and the vascular plants or tracheophytes. The nonvascular plants lack vascular tissues and do not have true roots, stems, and leaves. Therefore, the nonvascular plants have root like, stem like, and leaf like structures. General characteristics of Bryophytes Bryophytes are small plants, many are only 1 cm tall and a few exceed 2 cm. They are often called amphibians of plant kingdom. All bryophytes are photosynthetic and manufacture their own food. They have multicellular sex organs. Some of their sporophytes are green and prominent as compared to gametophyte. In many bryophytes the spores are not enclosed within gametophyte tissue, others are covered at maturity. The main features of bryophytes are: (1) They lack specialized vascular tissues. (2) Multicellular sex organs produce embryo. (3) Sporophytes are always smaller and obtain their food from the gametophyte. (4) Their life cycles involve alternation of the generation. (5) Bryophytes are also called amphibious plants because they need water for development, existence and reproduction. Life Cycle of Moss The moss plants show two generations the sporophyte and the gametophyte, which regularly alternate with each other. It is known as alternation of generation. The life cycle is completed when the plant passes through these two generations. The matured green shoot is the gametophyte. It produces gametes and reproduces by sexual union. The sex organ is at the apex of the shoot. The male sex organ is known as antheridium and the female sex organ as archegonium. The sex organs are intermixed with sterile multicellular hair like structures, known as paraphyses. The two sex organs may occur on the same plant, i.e., monoecious or on two separate plants, i.e., dioecious. The sporophyte consists of a foot which is embedded in the tissue of the gametophyte and a stalk or seta with a capsule at the tip. Spores are formed in the sporophyte by meiosis, thus the spores are haploid. The spore germinates to form an algal like structure called protonema, having bud and branches. The buds develop into gametophyte. In the mature gametophyte the archegonia and antheridia are produced. The Land Adaptations of Bryophytes The land adaptive characteristics exhibited by nonvascular plants are: The multicellular plant body and conservation of water: The plant body of liverworts called thallus is very small and multicellular consists of hundreds of cells, e.g., Marchantia.

Only the cells of the upper epidermis are exposed to the atmosphere. Some cells are photosynthetic cells. The second zone consists of storage cells. Water cannot enter these cells because the upper epidermal cells contain cutin, which is a wax like water resistant substance. Pores and air chambers: The upper surface of thallus contains pores, which lead into air chambers containing photosynthetic cells. CO2 is absorbed by large amount through pores and reaches into the air chambers. From air chambers CO2 then diffuses into the photosynthetic cells. Along with CO2 being absorbed, evaporation of water may occur through the pores. Absorption of water by rhizoids: The structures for absorption of water in moss and liverworts are rhizoids. These are present on the lower surface of the Marchantia thallus. Rhizoids are long filamentous structures. They are unicellular and are extensions of the cell of the lower epidermis. Rhizoids increase surface area for absorption of water from the soil and also help in anchorage. Production of gametes: When two different types of gametes are produced, it is called heterogamy. Sperms and ova are produced in archegonium and antheridium respectively in terrestrial plants, e.g., Moss, Marchantia etc. The sperms are flagellated and require water for reaching egg. The egg is large and nonmotile. It contains large amount of food which is needed to nourish the early stages of the developing embryo after fertilization. Due to water requirement for fertilization they cannot live away from water. Embryo Formation: The fertilization is inside the archegonium. The zygote divides to form the embryo which is retained inside the archegonium. The chances of survival of embryo are increased as it is protected by the wall of the archegonium. Embryo is present in all bryophytes and vascular plants. Alternation of Generations: The mosses and liverworts have a life cycle with alternating gametophyte and sporophyte generations. It increases the chances of survival of the plants on land. Importance of Bryophytes Mosses play an important role in their environment. They hold the soil and prevent erosion. They provide food for animals, especially birds and wild animals. Commercially the most important mosses are the peat mosses. Their partially decomposed remains are harvested as peat and used as a soil conditioner. When added to sandy soils peat moss helps to hold and retain moisture. SEEDLESS VASCULAR PLANTS The vascular plants include ferns and their allies, gymnosperms and angiosperms. The vascular tissue consists of xylem and phloem. The vascular plants have true roots, stems and leaves. Xylem, with its strong walled cells, supports the body of the plant against the pull of gravity. The leaves are covered by a waxy cuticle. Leaves have small pores called stomata. The sporophyte generation is diploid and dominant in vascular plants. The vascular plants are widely distributed. The seedless vascular plants (ferns and their allies) disperse the species by producing windblown spores. When the spores germinate, a relatively large gametophyte is formed which is independent of the sporophyte for its nutrition.

In these plants, flagellated sperms are released by antheridia and swim in a film of external water to the archegonia, where fertilization occurs. Because the seedless vascular plants are not closely related, each type is placed in its own division. The seedless vascular plants include whisk ferns (division Psilotophyta), club mosses (division Lycopodophyta), horsetails (division Equisetophyta), and ferns (division Pteridophyta). PsilopsidaWhisk ferns The group psilopsida includes the simplest known vascular plants known as whisk ferns, named for their resemblance to whisk brooms. The whisk fern lack true roots but bear underground stems called rhizomes that bear rhizoids. Aerial stems have no true leaves, they have only tiny scales. The stems branch repeatedly and carry on photosynthesis. Sporangia are present at the tips of the branches. Most members of this group are extinct. Example of extinct group is Rhynia. Psilotum is the most common living example. Evolution of leaf in vascular plants In vascular plants there are two types of leaves: (a) Single veined leaves (b) Many veined leaves. Single veined leaves are small and scale like. They have single vascular strand. Therefore they are called single or one veined leaves or microphyllous leaves e.g., club mosses (Lycopodium). Many veined leaves are large true leaves having prominent blade. As many veins and vascular bundles are present so they are called many veined leaves or megaphyllous leaves, e.g., Ginkgo etc. There is no fossil record showing the evolution of single veined leaves. However two hypotheses have been advanced to explain their origin: (a) out-growth hypothesis (b) reduction hypothesis. According to out-growth hypothesis single veined leaf originated as an outgrowth from the naked stem of primitive plant. The outgrowth had a single vascular strand. With increase in size, vascular tissues were developed for the transportation of food, water and support. Thus vascular strand extended from main vascular cylinder of the stem to a single veined leaf. It is believed that the early vascular plants had naked stems with forked branches found in early vascular plants e.g., Rhynia. According to reduction hypothesis the forked branches were changed to a single plane known as planation. The branches became flat and spaces between the branches and vascular tissues became filled with photosynthetic tissues called webbing. The structure resembles superficially to the webbed foot of the duck and thus a many veined leaf evolved. Lycopsida-Club Mosses The plant body consists of a branching rhizome which sends up aerial stems less than 30 cm tall. Tightly packed scale like leaves cover the stem and branches of the plants. The leaves are microphylls, having only one strand of vascular tissue. In club mosses the sporangia are born on terminal clusters of leaves called strobili which are club shaped. They are only living plants to have microphylls. The familiar members of this group belong to genera Lycopodium and Selaginella. Sphenopsida-Horsetails Sphenopsida, commonly known as horsetails, are found in waste and wet places. This group includes more fossil plants than living one. Today there is only one genus, Equisetum.

Pteropsida-Ferns Ferns belong to the group pteropsida, subgroup or class filicinae, which are most abundant group of seedless vascular plants in warm and moist tropical regions. Ferns range in size from reduced aquatic forms less than a centimetre, to a tree fern that may have trunks more than 24 metres tall, with leaves up to 5 metres or more in length. Except few all the ferns are homosporous. Sporophyte generation is much larger, more conspicuous, and more complex than the gametophyte. Sporophyte is completely independent. Sporangia are foliar, i.e., attached to leaves or fronds. When the frond is young and immature, it is coiled. This pattern of development is called circinate vernation. It is an important feature of ferns. Importance of peat bogs Sphagnum moss often grows in wet, spongy places forming dense mats. Such places are called bogs. One of the distinctive features of this moss is a presence of large empty cells. This feature makes peat moss particularly beneficial to humans. When added to sandy soils, for example, peat moss helps to hold and retain moisture. In bogs, the dead Sphagnum accumulates and do not decay. This accumulated moss called peat is used as fuel. Life Cycle of Fern Life cycle of Adiantum (Maidenhair fern) contains two generations i.e., sporophyte and gametophyte. Both of these generations are independent. Sporophyte generation Sporophyte of Adiantum produces vegetative leaves at start. At later stages, fertile leaves also start producing along with vegetative leaves. Fertile leaves produce sori (singular: sorus) on their underside. Sori are group of sporangia. These sori are covered with a flap of tissue called false indusium. A mature sporangium is flattened, spherical or ellipsoidal. It consists of a stalk and a rounded structure called capsule. Capsule is covered with single layered wall. Wall contains two portions: annulus and stomium. Annulus portion contains cells with thick cell walls. Stomium consists of cell with thin cell walls. This is the site for bursting of sporangium. Within sporangium, spores are produced by meiosis of spore mother cells. Many spores are produced. Spore wall contains two layers exine and intine. At maturity, the wall of sporangia burst. Sporangium becomes dry, so annulus shrinks which exerts pressure on stomium cells. Stomium is the weak point, so sporangia get burst from this region, thus causing the dispersal of spores. After falling on suitable place, exine of spore bursts and intine elongates to produce rhizoids and protonema. Gametophyte generation Protonema develops into gametophyte called prothallus. It is heart shaped. It has a notch, where apical cell is present. Rhizoids develop from underside of gametophyte for anchorage and absorption. Gametophyte contains chloroplasts, so carry out photosynthesis. It is independent. Two kinds of organs archegonia and antheridia are produced on gametophyte. Archegonium is a flask like structure with two portions i.e., venter and neck. Venter contains egg and neck canal cells. Antheridia are globose structures; in which antherozoids are produced. Antherozoids when get mature have two flagella.

During sexual reproduction antherozoids after releasing from antheridia travel through water chemotactically towards archegonia. Antherozoids fertilize the egg inside archegonia. Resultant zygote develops into embryo. Embryo starts divisions to form sporophyte. Sporophyte depends upon gametophyte at start but soon it becomes independent. The life cycle of fern shows heteromorphic alternation of generation. Importance of Seedless Vascular Plants Lycopodium and Selaginella are chiefly grown as ornamental plants. Ducks and other water fowls feed upon the rhizome of lycopsida sp. The ferns are mostly ornamental plants of gardens and greenhouses. Some of them are used in the preparation of bouquets. Stems and leaves of tree ferns are used for building materials. Some genera are edible. Some ferns yield a drug, which is utilized for removing the intestinal-parasites. Practically all the members of the seedless vascular plants have contributed extensively to coal formation. SEED PLANTS The two groups of seed bearing vascular plants are the gymnosperms and angiosperms. The seeds of gymnosperm are produced exposed on the surface of the sporophylls that make up cones. The seeds of angiosperms are usually enclosed by a fruit and produced from a flower. Evolution of Seed Seed may be considered as a fertilized megasporangium. It has integument around it. During course of evolution seed has passed through the following stages. Heterospory: Seed plants are heterosporous i.e., produce microspore and megaspore respectively. The megaspore grows into a female gametophyte and the microspore grows into a male gametophyte. The megaspores of the seed plants remain inside the sporangium, where the megaspore develops into a tiny female gametophyte. Evolution of pollen tube: The evolution of pollen tube parallels the evolution of seeds. The egg produced inside the female gametophyte is very well protected in the sporangium. It is so well protected that flagellated sperm would not have the slightest chance of ever reaching an egg. This obstacle has been overcome by the development of pollen tubes. Once the pollen grain reaches the cone or flower, it germinates. The germinated pollen grain is a tiny male gametophyte. It produces a long pollen tube, which grows to the ovule and then digests its way through the protecting layers to the enclosed egg. Evolution of Integument around the Megasporangium and Seed: In carboniferous period fern like plants were present. The sporophyte of these plants had little protective branch like outgrowths, surrounding the megasporangium. During evolution the outgrowths fused together forming integument, enclosing the megasporangium. Megaspore is retained in the megasporangium. This modified structure is called an ovule. The fertilized ovule evolved into seed because of retention of developing embryo. Gymnosperms (naked seed plants) The plant body of gymnosperms may be tall, woody, perennial trees or shrubs. The plant body is a sporophyte, differentiated into stem, leaves and root. The stem is branched with an exception of Cycas, which is unbranched. Gymnosperms have two types of leaves. The foliage leaves bear sporangia. Reproductive structures are usually borne in the cones on which sporophylls are spirally arranged.

The leaves are of two kinds i.e., scale leaves and foliage leaves. Foliage leaves may be needle like, linear or broad. The leaves are evergreen with sunken stomata. Venation is simple. The arrangement of leaves is either spiral or cyclic. Leaves exhibit xerophytic features like thick and tough cuticle, sunken stomata, presence of wax on the surface. Xylem consists of tracheids and lacks vessels. Wood parenchyma and wood fibres are generally absent. Companion cells are also absent. Male and female sporophylls are arranged on separate cones i.e., microsporophyll and megasporophylls, i.e., produce microspores and megaspores respectively. They are heterosporous. Sporophyte and gametophytic generation are quite distinct. Uses of gymnosperms Pine seeds like chilghoza are eaten as dry fruits. Ephedrine, a drug from Ephedra is used for the relief of asthma and other respiratory ailments. Conifers are a source of soft wood for construction, packing, plywood, board and for making paper. Cycads are cultivated as ornamental plants, a wild cycad, serves as a source of sago. It is obtained as a liquid state and then solidifies to form small granules. Resins, turpentine, tar and oils are obtained from conifers. Angiosperms (enclosed seed plants) Angiosperms are the flowering plants. Their seeds are enclosed by fruits. The leaves bearing ovules are folded and joined at the margins to form ovaries. The ovary after fertilization is changed into fruit. This is exceptionally a large and successful group of plants which is divided into two groups dicots and monocots. They have common characters, like, vascular tissues, differentiated plant body, flowers, fruits, and seeds. The two groups may be differentiated as shown in table. Life Cycle of a Flowering Plant All plants show alternation of generations in the flowering plants. The sporophyte, a diploid plant, alternates with haploid inconspicuous gametophytic generation. The anthers and carpels act as male and female parts respectively. A typical anther when fully developed contains 2 to 4 elongated sacs called pollen sacs. The pollen sacs contain pollen grains. When anther is developing, mitotic divisions produces microspore mother cells inside it. As a result of meiosis in a diploid mother cell, four haploid microspores are produced. A microspore then divides mitotically into a two celled, pollen grain. A tough wall develops around the pollen grain, which protects the contents of the pollen grain from drying out. Cells on the surface of stigma secrete a sticky nutrient fluid containing sugar and other substances. After pollination the pollen grains germinate on the stigma. Each pollen grain produces a long, thin walled pollen tube. The pollen tube grows down, through the tissues of the stigma, style and ovary until it reaches the ovule. As the pollen tube develops, the two nuclei of the pollen grain move into it. The two nuclei are called generative nucleus and the pollen tube nucleus. Generative nucleus divides to form two somewhat elongated sperms. The tube nucleus is located near the tip of the pollen tube with two sperms following behind.

The pollen tube, containing tube nucleus and the two sperms (male gametes), is the male gametophyte. The ovule is an egg shaped structure attached by a stalk, to the inside of the ovary. Depending upon the species of the plant involved, an ovary may have one, two, several or many thousands of ovules. The ovule has an opening called micropyle. Megaspore mother cell of the ovule undergoes meiosis to produce four haploid cells. Only one of these cells survives. The surviving cell is called the megaspore which divides by mitosis three times to produce eight haploid nuclei. This structure is called embryo sac. Wall formation takes place and these nuclei are converted into cells. The cells of embryo sac are antipodal cells, polar nuclei, synergids and egg. The embryo sac having these cells are called female gametophyte. Antipodal cells are three in number and are present at the opposite end of the micropyle. They have no function and sooner or later get disorganized. Synergids are two cells present at micropylar end. These help in fertilization by guiding the pollen tube and after fertilization is over these get disorganized. Polar nuclei are two in number, present at the centre. Egg is present at micropylar end and is present between the two synergids. When pollen tube reaches the embryo sac, the tip of the tube ruptures. One of the two sperms fuses with the egg to form a zygote. The other sperm fuses with the fusion nucleus to form a primary endosperm nucleus. This only occurs in the flowering plants. Seeds and fruits: The development of embryo takes place in the ovule. After fertilization fusion nucleus develops into an embryonic plant, which consists of three sets of haploid chromosomes, i.e., it is triploid. The triploid nucleus divides and develops into an endosperm. It is triploid tissue. The endosperm divides, enlarges and is used as stored food for the young embryo. After fertilization the formation of embryo and endosperm tissue takes place simultaneously. Meanwhile the ovule increases in size. The embryo consists of: (i) One or two cotyledons, (ii) epicotyl (iii) hypocotyl. Both epicotyl and hypocotyl are the parts of the rod like axis attached to the cotyledons. In some plants cotyledons digest and absorb endosperm as they mature into seed. The ovary wall enlarges and ripens to become the fruit. Differences between dicots and monocots Leaves: Broad, generally bifacial with reticulate venation in dicots. Long narrow, lanceolate, monofacial with parallel venation in monocots. Stem: Vascular bundle in ring, vascular cambium is present which gives secondary growth in dicots. Vascular bundles scattered, vascular cambium usually absent so no secondary growth occurs in monocots. Root: Primary root is a tap root which develops lateral root in dicots. Adventitious roots arise from the base of stem, and give rise to a fibrous root system in monocots. Flowers: Typically tetra or pentamerous, calyx and corolla usually differ from each other. Flowers are usually insect pollinated in dicots. Parts usually in three i.e., trimerous.

No distinction between calyx and corolla. Flowers are often air pollinated in monocots. Examples: Rose, pea, buttercup etc in dicots. Lilies, orchids, grasses, wheat, rice in monocots. Adaptations of angiosperms on land Roots, stems and leaves: The vascular tissue contains vessels as well as tracheids. Leaves are broad, expanded and provided with a dense network of veins. The broad leaves are efficient in absorbing light for photosynthesis. The cuticle covering the aerial parts helps to protect the plant from drying in the terrestrial environment. Angiosperms have conquered all kinds of habitats and some have even returned to water. Flowers: The reproductive organs are enclosed in flowers which are modified for wind and insects pollination. Fertilization takes place through pollen tube independent of external water. Double fertilization increased survival success. Following fertilization the ovules located in ovaries develop into seeds. Ovary wall is transformed into a fruit. Fruits provide protection for seeds and a mechanism for wide dispersal. Inflorescence Flowers are borne either single or in clusters. A flower is said to be solitary when it is borne singly, e.g., shoe flower. Flowers borne in clusters along with the stem and associated whorls constitute inflorescence. Depending upon the arrangement of flowers, inflorescence is classified into (a) Racemose (b) Cymose (c) Compound. Racemose inflorescence: In this type the main axis of inflorescence does not end in a flower but it continues to grow and give off flowers laterally. The basal flowers are older and upper are younger. e.g., mustard. Cymose inflorescence: In this type the main axis terminates in a flower but the lateral buds continue to grow in the same manner. The flowers are formed in basipetal succession, i.e., the basal flowers are younger and upper flowers are older, e.g., Dianthus (pink). Compound inflorescence: In compound inflorescence the main axis of the inflorescence branches repeatedly in a racemose manner and each branch bears flowers in a racemose or cymose pattern, e.g., Cassia fistula. Significance of Angiosperms to Humans Angiosperms form the bulk of the food of man. Major cereals are wheat, rice, maize etc. Dry fruits are also eaten as dry fruits, e.g., groundnut, cashew nut, almonds, walnut, etc. Seeds rich in oil are called oil seeds. Oil seeds for cooking are obtained from groundnut, mustard, cotton seeds, rape seed etc. Spices include cinnamon, cloves, chillies, black pepper, cumin seeds, caraway, coriander, fennel. Tea, coffee and cocoa are important beverages obtained from flowering plants. Sugar is obtained from sugar beet and sugar cane roots. Many plants yield fodder for the cattle. Important fodder giving plants are berseem, shaftal, senji, etc. A large number of drugs are obtained from flowering plants. Some of the drugs are morphine and codeine from opium, quinine from cinchona. Important timber yielding plants are teak, sal, oak and sisso. Commercial cork is obtained from oak. Many plants provide us fibres for various uses. Textile fibres are obtained from cotton, rough fibres for making ropes and gunny bags are obtained from flax, hemp, jute etc.

Jute fibres are used to make ropes, bags, carpets, and mats etc. The husk of fruits of coconut is used for making coir, brooms and duster etc. A large number of flowering plants are grown in gardens and houses as ornamental plants. Common among them are roses, pansies, petunias, etc.

Enzymes 1 ENZYME STRUCTURE With the exception of ribozymes, all enzymes are globular proteins made up of one or more polypeptides. Ribozymes are enzymes composed of RNA and are found in ribosomes. For example, peptidyl transferase is a ribozyme which forms peptide bonds during protein synthesis. 4 Shape of Enzymes and Components of an Active Site Most protein enzymes have molecular weights ranging from about 10,000 to over one million. Such enzymes possess tertiary or quaternary structure. The catalytic activity of an enzyme is located in its active site, which is a specific, charge-bearing, three-dimensional cavity. The substrate (reactant) binds to the active site by non-covalent interactions such as hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions. The active site consists of 312 amino acids which may be scattered in the polypeptide chain but are brought together by secondary and tertiary folding of the protein molecule. The active site of aldolase consists of glycine, serine and alanine amino acids. The active site consists of two regions: (a) Binding site (b) Catalytic site Fig. 3.1: Active site grouping of amino acids of a polypeptide chain Some amino acids of the active site constitute the binding site, while others constitute the catalytic site. The shape of the active site is designed according to the substrate; therefore, only a particular substrate can attach to the active site. However, sometimes related substrates can also bind. Some enzymes require a non-protein part called cofactor. The cofactor not only helps in substrate binding but also participates in the catalytic process. The final shape of the active site is established after the attachment of the cofactor. An enzyme that requires a cofactor becomes active only when the cofactor is attached. This active enzyme is called holoenzyme. Without the cofactor, the protein part is inactive and is called apoenzyme. Some enzymes do not require cofactors but still show active and inactive forms. Pepsin is an example. It is secreted in inactive form called pepsinogen. When pepsinogen comes in contact with HCl in the stomach, the additional polypeptide fragment is removed and active pepsin is formed. How are enzymes formed? Enzymes are proteins and are synthesized according to the message encoded in DNA. Enzymes are produced inside living cells but retain catalytic activity even outside cells (in vitro). Nowadays enzymes are also produced using recombinant DNA technology. Types of Cofactors Cofactors may be inorganic or organic molecules. Inorganic cofactors include metal ions such as Fe², Mg², Ca², Zn² and Cu². These ions are loosely attached to enzymes. Organic cofactors are of two types: Coenzymes (loosely attached), e.g., ATP, NAD, FAD Prosthetic groups (permanently attached), e.g., iron-containing porphyrin ring in cytochromes Mechanism of Enzyme Action In an enzyme-catalyzed reaction, the substrate first binds to the active site forming an enzyme-substrate (ES) complex. The substrate is then converted into product forming enzyme-product (EP) complex. Finally, the product is released and the enzyme becomes free again.

E S ES EP E P The enzyme can create favorable local conditions (pH, charge, water concentration) inside the active site, making reactions more likely. For example, if a substrate is to be split, the enzyme may stretch the bond, making it easier to break. 4 Models of Enzyme Action Two models explain enzyme action. Lock and Key Model Proposed by Emil Fischer (1894). According to this model, the active site has a rigid shape complementary to the substrate. Only a specific substrate fits into the active site. The active site does not change shape during reaction. This model explains enzyme specificity and supports the idea that enzymes catalyze specific reactions only. Enzymes following this model are called non-regulatory enzymes. Fig. 3.3: Fischers Lock and Key hypothesis Enzymes Many enzymes show a broad range of specificity. When one enzyme can catalyze only one substrate, it is called absolute specificity, e.g., urease. Urea (Urease) Ammonia Carbon dioxide Induced Fit Model Daniel Koshland proposed the Induced Fit Model in 1959. According to this model, the active site of the enzyme is not rigid but flexible. When the substrate interacts with the enzyme, the shape of the active site is modified. The amino acids that make up the active site are molded into a precise shape which enables the enzyme to perform its catalytic function more effectively. The change induced in the shape of the active site is responsible for the conversion of substrate into product. As soon as the reaction is completed, the active site regains its original shape. This flexibility of the active site allows more than one type of related substrates to be attached, and therefore an enzyme can carry out more than one type of related reactions. An example is carbonic anhydrase, which can add oxygen to hemoglobin as well as control the formation of carbonic acid and bicarbonates in blood. Enzymes that follow the induced fit mechanism are called regulatory or homeostatic enzymes, for example hexokinase. Hb O₂ (Carbonic anhydrase) Oxyhaemoglobin CO₂ H₂O (Carbonic anhydrase) H₂CO₃ H HCO₃ Products are released and the enzyme is ready to catalyze a new reaction. Fig. 3.4: Koshlands Induced Fit model of enzyme action Energy of Activation Energy is required to cause molecules to react with one another. This energy is called energy of activation. In non-living systems, heat is often used to increase molecular motion and cause reactions. In living cells and organisms, enzymes lower the energy of activation required for chemical reactions. The excited state of molecules or intermediates is achieved by biochemical processes rather than heat. 3 FACTORS AFFECTING THE RATE OF ENZYMATIC ACTION The rate of enzymatic reaction is measured by the amount of substrate converted or the amount of product formed during a given period of time. The external conditions that affect the rate of enzyme action include temperature, pH, enzyme concentration and substrate concentration. Effect of Temperature Heat increases molecular motion. Therefore, substrate and enzyme molecules move faster and the probability of collision increases.

As a result, the rate of reaction increases. An increase of just 10C doubles the rate of reaction up to a certain limit. The temperature at which an enzyme shows maximum activity is called optimum temperature. If temperature is increased beyond the optimum level, the enzyme undergoes denaturation despite increased molecular motion. Secondary and tertiary structures of the enzyme are destroyed. Fig. 3.6(a): Effect of temperature on the rate of enzyme-controlled reaction When an enzyme is denatured, it unfolds and loses the precise structure of its active site. The temperature which causes denaturation of enzyme is called maximum temperature. Hydrogen bonds are most sensitive to temperature changes. Fig. 3.6(b): Optimum temperature for human enzymes and thermophilic bacteria Human enzymes have an optimum temperature of about 3738C, whereas enzymes of thermophilic bacteria living in hot springs have optimum temperatures around 70C or higher. These enzymes are used in biological washing powders for high-temperature washes. If temperature is reduced to near or below freezing point, enzymes become inactive but are not denatured. They regain catalytic activity when temperature rises again. This lowest temperature at which inactive enzyme becomes active is called minimum temperature. Effect of pH Each enzyme functions most effectively within a specific pH range called optimum pH. Enzyme conformation is sensitive to pH changes because pH affects the ionization of amino acid side chains involved in maintaining enzyme structure. A slight change in pH causes temporary inactivation, whereas extreme pH changes disrupt ionic bonds and lead to denaturation. Most enzymes function optimally at pH 68. Pepsin works best at pH 2 (acidic). Trypsin functions optimally at pH 8 (alkaline). Effect of Enzyme Concentration Provided that substrate concentration is high and conditions such as pH and temperature remain constant, the rate of enzyme-catalyzed reaction is directly proportional to enzyme concentration. One enzyme molecule can convert hundreds of substrate molecules into products. Increasing enzyme concentration increases the number of active sites, thus increasing reaction rate. This effect persists until equilibrium is reached. Fig. 3.8: Relationship between enzyme concentration and rate of enzyme-controlled reaction Effect of Substrate Concentration When enzyme concentration is constant and substrate concentration is increased, the rate of reaction increases initially. Eventually, the reaction reaches a maximum velocity (Vmax). Further increase in substrate concentration does not increase the reaction rate because all active sites of enzyme molecules are saturated. Fig. 3.9: Effect of substrate concentration on the rate of enzyme-controlled reaction 4 ENZYME INHIBITION Enzyme inhibition is a phenomenon in which enzyme activity is reduced or stopped. The molecules that bind to enzymes but are not converted into products are called enzyme inhibitors. Inhibition is a normal regulatory process in cells, but external inhibitors can be harmful. Examples include poisons, cyanides, antibodies, heavy metals and sulpha drugs. Competitive Inhibition In competitive inhibition, inhibitor competes with substrate for the active site. Competitive inhibitors are structurally similar to substrates. Competitive inhibition is reversible. Increasing substrate concentration reduces inhibitor effect. Example: Succinate dehydrogenase is competitively inhibited by malonate. Fig.

3.10: Competitive inhibition Importance of competitive inhibitors: Supports Lock and Key model Explains enzyme specificity Used in drug design (e.g., sulphonamides) Non-Competitive Inhibition In non-competitive inhibition, the inhibitor binds to a site other than the active site called the allosteric site. This binding alters enzyme shape. Non-competitive inhibition may be reversible or irreversible. Irreversible inhibitors permanently denature enzymes. Examples include cyanides and heavy metals such as mercury and silver. These bind to sulfhydryl (SH) groups and disrupt disulfide bridges, destroying tertiary structure.
