The second function of a bacterial capsule is to promote the adhesion of the bacteria to living and inert surfaces and the third function is to facilitate the formation of adherent, glycocalyx-enclosed populations that are called biofilms. Biofilm bacteria can become difficult to kill, partly due to the presence of the glycocalyx material. Bacterial cell wall: Cell wall is the part of bacterial envelope. It is situated outer to the cell membrane.

It is composed of an inner layer of peptidoglycan and an outer lipoprotein membrane (found only in Gram negative bacteria). The peptidoglycan provides structural support and maintains the characteristic shape of the cell. The peptidoglycan layer is much thicker in Gram-positive than in Gram-negative bacteria. Some Gram-positive bacteria also have fibre of teichoic acid that protrudes outside the peptidoglycan, whereas Gram-negative bacteria do not have it. In contrast, the Gram-negative have a complex outer layer consisting of lipopolysaccharide and lipoprotein. The Gram-negative cell wall also contains a protein, the porins in outer membrane which act like pores for particular molecules. Lying between the peptidoglycan layer of cell wall and the cell membrane in Gram-negative bacteria is the periplasmic space which is the site of enzymes that degrade antibiotics. Pilus is present only in Gram negative bacteria. They allow bacterial cells to adhere to tissue and can help the bacterial cell resist attack from immune system cells in the human body. Bacterial cell membrane: The cell or plasma membrane lies beneath the cell wall which lacks cholesterols in lipid bilayer unlike eukaryotic plasma membrane. At certain points this membrane invaginates into the cytoplasm to form infolding, these are known as mesosomes. In addition to the control of transport of materials across the cell, bacterial plasma membrane also involves in cellular respiration, photosynthesis and DNA replication. Bacterial cytoplasm: The cytoplasm is a jelly like dense mass which lacks cytoskeleton. The ribosomes of bacteria are 70S. Bacterial cytoplasm may contain reserve food and waste products. Reserve food includes glycogen, fats, polyphosphate etc. Whereas, wastes may consist of alcohol, lactic acid, acetic acid etc. Bacterial genome: Nucleoid is the nuclear region of bacteria which is not separated from the cytoplasm by a nuclear membrane. It is seen in the electron microscope as an area lighter than the cytoplasmic contents. It consists of a large circular double stranded DNA molecule which is known as bacterial chromosome. Due to this single chromosome bacteria are considered as haploid organisms. A short duration of diploid state comes in their life cycle just before cell division when they replicate their DNA. Bacterial DNA differs from eukaryotic DNA as it is a circular molecule. The nuclear DNA controls growth and metabolic activities of bacteria. In addition to the nuclear DNA some bacteria also contain one or more extra nuclear small circular double stranded DNA molecules, the plasmids. They often contain genes for antibiotics or drug resistance and heavy metals resistance. Bacterial appendages: The structures that project from the surface of bacterial cell are called bacterial appendages that include flagella and pili or fimbriae. Flagella are long thread like structures which are used for locomotion. Bacterial flagella are composed of flagellin protein and lack microtubules. In this way they differ from eukaryotic flagella. Pili or fimbriae are tubular extensions of cell membrane and project through the cell wall.

They are composed of pilin protein and can only be seen by electron microscope and are found only on certain species of Gram negative bacteria. Pili are used to transfer genetic material during conjugation. The other function of pili is attachment on the surface of tissues of an infected person. Structure of Bacterial Flagellum Bacterial flagellum is non-contractile, and lacks microtubules unlike eukaryotic flagellum. It is about 20 nm diameter and up to 20 micrometer in length. It consists of three parts: a basal body, a hook and a filament. The basal body originates from cytoplasm just beneath the cell membrane. Gram-positive bacteria have one pair of discs whereas Gram-negative bacteria have two pairs of discs which anchors the flagellum in cell envelope. Central rod connects the discs. The hook is a short curved structure which connects the basal body to the filament. The filament is a hollow tube like structure which originates from the hook. The mechanism of movement of bacterial flagellum is quite different from eukaryotic flagella. The 360 rotation of paired discs of basal body enables the flagellum to rotate which in turn causes the cell to spin and move forward. Bacterial Spores and Cysts During late stage of growth, when essential nutrients are lacking in the environment or other conditions such as temperature, pH of the medium and availability of oxygen become unfavorable certain bacteria form resistant and metabolically dormant bodies. Depending on the type of bacteria, these bodies are divided into endospores, exospores, and cysts. Especially endospores are characterized by a complex structure and resistance to high temperatures. That is why this dormant form is capable of surviving for periods more than thousand years. The spore develops within the vegetative cell inside the cell wall, so it has been named endospore. The original cell forms a copy of its chromosome and surrounds it with a tough wall, forming the endospore. Water is removed from the endospore. The metabolism inside it stops. The rest of the original cell then disintegrates. The endospores germinate when their environmental conditions become favourable. On the other hand the Actinomycetes, which are a large group of spore-forming, Gram positive bacteria that grow by forming long tubules called filaments. Under nutrient poor condition these filaments differentiate into round thick walled resting structures termed exospores. In contrast to endospores, these structures are part of the reproductive process. Azotobacter species and several others are known to produce cysts which are dormant cells with thickened cells walls. Encystment (cyst formation) occurs when cell cytoplasm contracts and the cell wall thicken. Cysts are resistant to desiccation and chemicals, but cannot withstand high temperatures. MOTILITY IN BACTERIA Movement is an important aspect of bacterial life in that the organism moves towards higher concentrations of nutrients and away from toxic substances. This type of movement in response to chemical stimuli is called chemotaxis, and movement in response to light is called phototaxis.

Flagellar movement: Majority of bacilli and spirilla are motile by means of flagella while cocci are usually non-motile. The presence of flagella, their number and distribution on the cell surface are important characteristics for purposes of identification and classification of bacteria. When one or more flagella arise only from one or both ends of a rod or spiral shaped cell, the arrangement is termed polar. For example: if a bacterium possesses single flagellum at one end, called monopolar monotrichous; if the bacterium possesses single flagellum at both ends, is called bipolar monotrichous or amphitrichous. Similarly, if a bacterium possesses a pair of flagella at one end, called monopolar bitrichous; if the bacterium possesses a pair of flagella at both ends, is called bipolar bitrichous or amphibitrichous. But, if a tuft (more than two) of flagella is present at one end of a bacterium, called lophotrichous, and if a tuft of flagella is present at both ends of a bacterium, called amphilophotrichous. When, flagella arise randomly over the entire surface of the cell, the arrangement is termed peritrichous. Spirochaetal movement: A somewhat modified version of the bacterial flagellum is called axial filament. It is present in Spirochaete. The axial filament runs lengthwise between the bacterial inner membrane and outer membrane of the cell wall in periplasmic space. Spirochaetes can perform e.g., swimming, creeping or spinning type of movements with the help of axial filament. Gliding movement: Like spirochaetal movement, the gliding motility is also represented by some genera of cyanobacteria and myxobacteria. These organisms can move slowly over solid surfaces. They have filamentous structures either internally like axial filament of spirochetes or external like flagella of bacilli but they secrete a slimy substance like garden snails during movement. MODES OF NUTRITION IN BACTERIA Bacteria can be classified on the basis of method of obtaining energy and carbon. Broadly bacteria are either autotrophic or heterotrophic. Autotrophic bacteria: Autotrophic bacteria are generally called photosynthetic bacteria. Except cyanobacteria all the other photosynthetic bacteria contain unique type of chlorophyll called bacteriochlorophyll. The chlorophyll is incorporated in the membrane of cell. Unlike green plants, algae, and cyanobacteria they do not use water as reducing agent, and so do not produce oxygen. Instead they use hydrogen sulphide, which may be oxidized to produce granules of elemental sulphur. This sulphur may be oxidized to sulphuric acid. However, like green plants, the photosynthetic bacteria use the energy of sunlight to make carbohydrates from CO2. 2H2S CO2 --- (CH2O)n H2O 2S The examples of photosynthetic bacteria are green sulphur bacteria, green non-sulphur bacteria and purple sulphur bacteria. Chemoautotrophs: The chemoautotrophic bacteria make carbohydrates from inorganic substance. They do not use light energy. They oxidize inorganic substance. The energy produced by this oxidation reaction is then used to make carbohydrates. Sulphur bacteria oxidize sulphur to produce energy. The energy thus produced is used by bacteria to make carbohydrate (CH2O)n. The examples of chemoautotrophic bacteria are nitrifying bacteria, sulphur bacteria.

2H2S O2 --- 2S H2O Energy Energy 2H2S CO2 --- (CH2O)n H2O 2S Heterotrophic bacteria: Heterotrophic bacteria cannot synthesize their organic compounds from simple inorganic substances. They depend on the organic compounds present in the environment. There are three categories of heterotrophic bacteria: Obligate aerobic bacteria: These bacteria require oxygen for growth and are called aerobic bacteria, e.g., Pseudomonas. Obligate anaerobic bacteria: These bacteria grow in the absence of oxygen and are called anaerobic bacteria, e.g., Spirochete. Some are facultative bacteria e.g., E.coli which grow either in the presence or absence of oxygen. The bacteria which require low concentration of oxygen for growth are known as microaerophilic e.g., Campylobacter. Saprophytic bacteria: The bacteria which feed on the complex dead organic matter are called saprophytic bacteria, e.g., Pseudomonas. Azotobacter species are saprophytic. GROWTH AND REPRODUCTION IN BACTERIA If bacteria are provided with nutrients and the required environmental factors, they become active and grow. Phases of Bacterial Growth Bacterial growth takes place on two levels. On one level, a cell builds up protoplasm and increases its size: on the other level, the cell increases the number of cells in the population. Bacterial growth occurs in four major phases which can be represented by bacterial growth curve. Lag phase: In this phase there is increase in cell size but not multiplication. Time is required for adaptation (synthesis of new enzymes) to new environment. During this phase vigorous metabolic activity occurs but cells do not divide. Enzymes and intermediates are formed and accumulate until they are present in concentration that permits growth to start. Log or Exponential phase: In log or exponential phase, the number of cells increases exponentially with respect to time, i.e., the number of cells doubles with each doubling time. The average time required for the population, or the biomass, to double is known as the generation time or doubling time. The cells multiply at the maximum rate in this exponential phase, i.e., there is linear relationship between time and logarithm of the number of cells. This continues until one of two things happens: either one or more nutrients in the medium become exhausted, or toxic metabolic products accumulate and inhibit growth. Oxygen becomes limited for aerobic microorganisms. Stationary phase: In this phase, due to exhaustion of nutrients or accumulation of toxic products death rate becomes equal to the growth rate and the growth cease completely. The count remains stationary as a result of balance between multiplication and death rate. Death or decline phase: In death phase, the death rate exceeds the rate of multiplication of cells. The rate of cell death may be exponential. Methods of reproduction in bacteria Bacteria reproduce by asexual method. In true sense sexual reproduction is absent. These methods of genetic recombination are misleadingly called sexual reproduction. Asexual reproduction: The commonest type of asexual reproduction in bacteria is binary fission. Some bacteria reproduce by budding.

Binary fission: Binary fission is the commonest type of reproduction under favourable conditions in which a cell divides or splits into two similar daughter cells. During the process, the bacterial DNA gets attached to the cell membrane and undergoes replication. As the cell enlarges the two daughter DNA gets separated. A cross wall is formed between the separating daughter DNA. It divides the cell into two daughter cells. The daughter cells soon grow to maturity within 20 minutes and divide again. Budding: In case of budding, a protuberance, called bud, develops at one end of the cell. Genome replication occurs, and one copy of the genome gets into the bud. Then the bud enlarges, eventually becomes a daughter cell and finally gets separated from the parents cell. Genetic recombination (Parasexuality) In bacteria, there is no true sexual reproduction because there is no meiosis, fertilization and zygote. Instead, it involves transfer of a portion of genetic material from a donor cell to a recipient cell. This process is called genetic recombination or parasexuality. It occurs in three ways: conjugation, transduction and transformation. Conjugation: Conjugation is the transfer of genetic material from one bacterium to another bacterium by direct contact. The bacterium that transfer the DNA, is called donor and the bacterium that will receive the DNA, is called recipient. Usually a small ring of DNA, called plasmid rather than the main bacterial DNA is transferred. Transduction: The transfer of genetic material from one bacterium to another bacterium through a bacteriophage virus, is called transduction. Actually it occurs when a bacteriophage is replicated in a bacterial cell, at the time of assembly of its components a portion of host bacterium may be enclosed into the viral capsid. When such viruses cause infection to other bacterial cells the DNA fragment of the previous host bacterium is thus transferred to the new host bacterium. Transformation: When bacteria die or when they are reproducing very rapidly, they release fragments of their DNA into their immediate environment. Such DNA fragments may be up taken by other bacteria by means of diffusion in that environment. This process of absorption of DNA into a cell from its immediate environment is called transformation. As a result the cell is transformed into a new type of cell. These cells are called transformed cells. Mutations and Genetic Recombinations in Bacteria Offspring inherit identical copies of their parent's genes and are called clones. However, all bacteria can evolve by selection on changes to their genetic material that occur through mutation and genetic recombination. Mutation rates vary widely among different species of bacteria and even among different clones of a single species. Most heritable changes in bacterial genomes come from random mutation due to different errors in DNA replication. IMPORTANCE OF BACTERIA Bacteria are very important members of biodiversity from ecological and economic points of view.

Ecological Importance of Bacteria The ecological importance refers to the role of bacteria in environment, such as decomposition of dead/complex organic matter, humus formation to increase the fertility of soil, nitrogen fixation, bioremediation etc. Role of bacteria in decomposition of dead organic matter: Bacteria serve as recyclers of nature as they are involved in decomposition of dead organic matter in the environment. If the dead bodies are not decomposed, the essential nutrients present in their bodies would not be released in the environment. The organic compounds present in dead bodies might diminish all the carbon dioxide from the atmosphere if there were no decomposers present on earth. Can you imagine the situation if there were no carbon dioxide in the atmosphere? There would have been no photosynthesis in the plants and in the result no food would have been produced by plants. Bacteria play a very crucial role in environment through the decomposition of dead organic matter. Bacteria use them as a source of nutrients, and in turn help in recycling the organic compounds trapped in the dead bodies. Through this process, other organisms also get benefited, who can use the simpler inorganic compounds/nutrients released from the dead matter by various bacteria. Role of bacteria to increase soil fertility by humus formation and nitrogen fixation: The decaying organic matter of dead organisms is called humus. It contains nutrients for the growth of plants. It also increases the water holding capacity of soil. Bacteria and fungi are the only organisms that decompose dead organic matter. Bacteria take part in humus formation. Nitrogen is the essential element for plants for their growth and metabolism. Atmospheric nitrogen cannot be used by plants as they cannot inhale nitrogen directly. Atmospheric nitrogen can be available to the plants through soil in the form of nitrates with the help of nitrogen fixing bacteria. Some plants (leguminous Plants) have a mutualistic association of bacteria (Rhizobium bacteria) living into their tissues for this purpose. Role of bacteria in removal or degradation of environmental pollutants: The removal or degradation of environmental pollutants by using living organisms is called bioremediation. It involves the use of many bacteria that either naturally love to eat certain toxins or have been genetically altered to give them the taste for toxins. Scientists are using microbes to clean sites of contaminants such as oil, radioactive waste and mercury. Economic Importance of Bacteria The economic importance of bacteria refers to the role of bacteria in research and technology, plant diseases and in human diseases. Role of bacteria in research and technology: When we think of bacteria, we usually think about the illness it can cause and our need to get rid of it. However, bacteria play a lot of positive roles in our lives which are unknown to many of us. Bacteria play an important role in many technological fields, mainly in biological research, mining, medicine, production of food products, plastics synthesis and sewage treatment. The overall commercial worth of bacteria in these operations is immense.

Bacteria have been used and being continuously used in the study of genetics and genetic engineering. Bacteria were used as model organism in number of famous experiments such as the discovery of DNA as heredity material, discovery of semi conservative replication of DNA and etc. Many components of bacterial cell are also being used as tools in genetic engineering experiments. The miners can extract metal from low grade ores in an eco-friendly way by using certain bacteria. Bacteria are useful to mankind is in the production of complex organic molecules that are of use in small amounts as part of the normal process of living, these include antibiotics, vitamins, amino acids and enzymes. In addition to these compounds, the dairy products such as yogurt, cheese, butter etc. are also produced with the help of bacteria. Now a day biodegradable plastic is being made by using bacteria. Owing to their characteristics of degrading harmful chemicals and pollutants, bacteria are nowadays used for treatment of waste water. Role of bacteria in causation of diseases and spoilage of food: Despite a lot of benefits some bacteria are harmful for us. Parasitic bacteria attack organisms and cause various diseases. Many human diseases are caused by bacteria. Bacteria cause decay of leather, fabrics etc. Bacteria spoil the food materials by decomposition. Some bacterial diseases in man such as cholera, typhoid, tuberculosis and pneumonia are briefly described here. Cholera: Symptoms: The symptoms include severe diarrhoea, vomiting, dehydration, weight loss, loss of skin turgidity, hypotension and intense muscle cramps. Cause: The causative agent is Vibrio cholerae. Transmission: It is transmitted through contaminated water and food. Treatment: Rehydration, Doxycycline antibiotic is used. Prevention: Use of safe and boiled water, sanitary disposal of sewage, avoid contaminated water, maintain personal hygiene, hand washing, immunization, control flies, eat cooked food and use safe water. Typhoid: Symptoms: The symptoms include fever, tender abdomen and spleen occur. Causative agent: The causative agent is Salmonella typhi. Transmission: Through fecal-oral route and carrier. Treatment: Ciprofloxacin antibiotic should be used. Prevention: Proper sanitation, safe drinking water, immunization by public health and personal hygiene. Prevention: Vaccination is effective prevention of typhoid. Tuberculosis: Symptoms: The symptoms include mild fever, tiredness and weakness, dry hacking cough and chest pain which increases on coughing, night sweats, weight loss, anorexia, anemia and bloody stained sputum. Cause: The causative agent is Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Transmission: It spreads through droplets. Treatment: Multiple-drug therapy is used during the long 6 to 9 month duration of treatment. However a new effective technique of DOTS (directly observed treatment short course) of only two months durations is also being used. Prevention: BCG Vaccine (Bacillus Calmette-Guerin) can be used. Pneumonia: Symptoms: Pneumonia often begins with sudden chill, cough and pleuritic pain. Sputum is red brown rusty colour. Cause: The causative agent is Streptococcus pneumoniae. Transmission: It spreads through droplets. Treatment: Antibiotics are used. Bacterial diseases in plants: The important bacterial plant diseases are leaf spots, blights, soft rots, wilts and galls.

Leaf spot disease: Symptoms: Brown to white spots on leaves. Cause: It is caused by Xanthomonas campestris on cabbage and Pepper. Prevention: Prevention of contact between pathogen and the host, use of disease free seeds. Blight disease: The blight is termed blight in maize, rice and oat etc. Cause: Xanthomonas oryzae Causes blight disease in rice. Prevention: Disease free seeds, eradication of diseased plant by physical method. Soft rots disease: Soft rots may involve removal of a part of the plant. Cause: Corynebacterium sepedonicum causes soft rot in potatoes. Prevention: Use disease free planting material. Wilt disease: It is widespread. Cause: Pseudomonas solanacearum causes wilt in potatoes and tomatoes. Prevention: Crop rotation, remove of diseased plants. Galls: Galls are outgrowth mostly small but may be very large in size. Cause: Rhizobium leguminosarum causes small galls called root nodules in leguminous plants. Prevention: Crop rotation, removal of diseased plants etc. THE BACTERIAL FLORA OF HUMANS There are approximately ten times as many bacterial cells as human cells in the human body, with large numbers of bacteria on the skin and in the digestive tract. Normal flora is the term used to describe the various bacteria (and fungi) that are permanent residents of certain body parts, especially the skin, oropharynx, colon and vagina. Benefits of the bacterial flora to humans The members of some normal flora play a role in the maintenance of health and the causation of disease in three ways: They can cause disease, especially in immunocompromised and weak, feeble individuals. They cause disease when they are introduced into unprotected areas; although they are nonpathogens in their usual anatomic location, they can be pathogens in other parts of the body. They constitute a protective host defense mechanism. The normal nonpathogenic resident bacteria occupy attachment sites on the skin and mucosa that can interfere with colonization by pathogens. The inhibition of the growth of pathogens is called colonization resistance. They may serve a nutritional function. The normal bacteria produce several B vitamins and vitamin K. Poorly nourished people who are treated with oral antibiotics can suffer vitamin deficiencies as a result of the reduction in the normal flora. CONTROL OF HARMFUL BACTERIA Bacteria can be controlled by chemical and physical methods. Chemical methods: Antiseptics, disinfectants and chemotherapeutic agents are used as chemical methods for microbial control. Antiseptics: The chemical substances used on living tissues that inhibit the growth of microorganisms are called antiseptics. Disinfectants: Oxidizing and reducing agents are important chemical agents for disinfection, e.g., disinfectants that is halogens and phenols, hydrogen peroxide, potassium permanganate, alcohol and formaldehyde etc. These chemicals inhibit the growth of vegetative cells and are used on nonliving material. Chemotherapeutic agents: Chemotherapeutic agents are chemicals and antibiotics that destroy the natural defence and stop the growth of bacteria and other microbes in the living tissue, e.g., sulphonamide, tetracycline, penicillin etc. Physical methods: Sterilization process is the process in which physical agents like steam, dry heat, gas, filtration and radiation are used to control bacteria.

Sterilization is destructive to all life forms. This process is used to sterilize large scale products. It is also used to preserve food items on commercial scale and usually used in microbiological labs for control of microbes. High temperature is usually used for sterilization. Radiations below 300 nm are effective in killing microbes. Gamma rays are also used for sterilization. Heat sensitive compounds like antibiotics, serum, hormones, enzymes, etc., can be sterilized by means of membrane filters. Pasteurization is heating at temperature enough to kill non-spore forming pathogenic bacteria, e.g., milk is pasteurized at 71 C for 16 seconds and then cooled. Food preservation: Food can be preserved for several weeks to several months, e.g., by drying, salting and freezing. In dry condition bacteria may not grow, e.g., dry fruits. Adding preservatives inhibit the growth of bacteria. Acid is added to many foods. Salt is added in high concentration. Contents of salt are increased so that water in the food is not enough for bacteria to grow. Some chemicals like potassium metabisulphite are added. Pickles, sauces, jams and breads are preserved by such methods.

Protists and Fungi PROTISTS: THE EVOLUTIONARY RELATIONSHIP Vast assortment of living forms, variations in size, shape, methods of reproduction, modes of nutrition, and life styles make it difficult for taxonomists to assign protists to a single kingdom. That is why the members of this kingdom do not have a common ancestor. Polyphyletic Origin of Protists Kingdom Protista is a polyphyletic group of organisms; that is, protists do not share a common ancestor. This hypothesis is based upon the variations exhibited by them in cell structure, ways of obtaining nutrients, mode of life, habitat, methods of reproduction and means of locomotion. Variations exhibited by protists The protists show variations in size, methods of obtaining nutrients, mode of life, and locomotion. Size: The size varies considerably within the protist kingdom, from microscopic protozoa to giant kelps, which are brown algae that can reach 75 metres in length. Although most protists are unicellular, some have a colonial organization (a colony is a loose aggregation of cells), some are coenocytic (multinucleate but not multicellular), and some are multicellular. Unlike fungi, plants and animals, multicellular protists have relatively simple body forms without specialized tissues. Methods of obtaining nutrients: These differ widely in kingdom protista. The autotrophic protists, e.g., the algae have chlorophyll and photosynthesize as plants do. Some of the heterotrophic protists, e.g., the water molds, obtain their food by absorption as fungi do. Other heterotrophs, i.e., the protozoa and slime molds resemble animals i.e., they ingest food derived from the bodies of other organisms. Mode of life: It shows that many protists are free living while others form symbiotic association with different organisms. These associations range from mutualism, a more or less equal partnership in which both organisms benefit, to parasitism in which one organism lives on or inside another and is metabolically dependent on it. Most protists are aquatic and live in oceans or freshwater. They make up a part of the plankton. Reproduction: Reproduction is quite varied in the kingdom protists. All protists reproduce asexually and many reproduce sexually with both meiosis and syngamy (the union of gametes). Sexual protists do not develop multicellular sex organs, nor do they form embryos. Locomotion: Many protists are motile at some stage of their life cycle and have various means of locomotion. It may be accomplished by amoeboid motion, i.e., by extensions of pseudopodia, or by cilia or flagella. Many protists use a combination of flagellar and amoeboid motion. CATEGORIES OF PROTISTS Protozoa: The Animal Like Protists Protozoa comes from the Latin word meaning first animals. This form protozoa is used today to designate an informal group of animal like protists. Protozoa ingest food, lack cell wall and have centrioles. Body of the protozoa is of a typical eukaryotic cell and consists of one cell containing all the structures necessary to perform the functions of life. Protozoa have organelles called vacuoles to perform special function. The food vacuoles when they are fused with lysosomes. Freshwater protozoans have contractile vacuoles for the elimination of water.

Reproduction takes place by asexual and sexual. The organs of locomotion are pseudopodia, e.g., Amoeba, Cilia, e.g., Paramecium, Flagella, e.g., Trypanosoma, the parasitic protozoans do not have any specific means of locomotion, e.g., Plasmodium (malarial parasite). Regeneration is common in protozoans. Protozoans form resistant cyst to overcome unfavourable conditions. The protozoans have been excluded from kingdom animalia due to their unicellular cell structure as rest of the animals are multicellular. Based upon means of locomotions, the protozoans are further classified into sarcodina, mastigophora, ciliophora and sporozoa. Sarcodina: These protozoans have cytoplasmic extensions i.e., pseudopodia as their locomotory structures. The sarcodines are mostly aquatic. Some of them are found in freshwater and have no shell, e.g., Amoeba proteus (free living) and Entamoeba histolytica (causes amoebic dysentery in human). While other are found in marine water and have shell either made up of calcium carbonate (e.g., Foraminifera) or of silica (e.g., Actinopods). Zooflagellates: Protozoans that move by means of flagella are called zooflagellates. Trypanosoma is a human parasitic zooflagellate causes sleeping sickness. Choanoflagellate is marine or freshwater zooflagellate. It is sessile and remains attached by a stalk. Flagellum is surrounded by a delicate collar which resembles the collar cell of sponges. Ciliophora: These protozoans have hair like extensions called cilia and have two types of nuclei. Ciliates differ from the other protozoans in having two types of nuclei, many small diploid micronuclei that function in sexual process and a single large polyploid macronucleus that controls cell metabolism and growth. (e.g., Paramecium). Sporozoa/Apicomplexans: These are parasitic protozoans. They lack locomotory structures for locomotion but can move by flexing of body wall (undulating movement). At some stage of their lives, they develop a spore, a small infective agent transmitted to the next host. Many apicomplexans complete their lifecycle in two hosts. (e.g., Plasmodium (malarial parasite). Algae: The Plant like Protists Algae (singular: alga) are found in freshwater ponds, lakes, streams, growing on the trunks of trees and in the sea. The body of algae may be unicellular, filamentous, colonial or multicellular. The multicellular algae may have a structure that is branched or leaf like but lacks the vascular tissues and roots, stems and leaves. The body of multicellular algae is called thallus. The photosynthetic pigments found in algae are green chlorophylls (e.g., red algae), xanthophyll and red phycoerythrin. The reserve food material is starch and stored in all groups of algae. Algal cell wall is made up of cellulose. Types of algae: On the basis of pigments, storage products and cell wall composition, algae are classified into many groups. Some of them are following: Euglenoids: The euglenoids are small unicellular freshwater organisms that do not have cell wall unlike other groups of algae similarly some of them are colorless and heterotrophs. Euglenoids have chlorophyll (a and b) and carotenoids. (e.g., Euglena). Dinoflagellates: Most dinoflagellates are unicellular. Their cells are often covered with shells of interlocking cellulose plates deposited with silicates. Some dinoflagellates are known to have occasional population explosions or blooms.

These blooms may colour the water orange, red or brown and are known as red tide. This is because of the presence of a carcinogenic compound, called saxitoxin. Dinoflagellates have chlorophyll (a and c) and carotenoids. Diatoms: They are microscopic unicellular algae in the oceans. This makes diatoms very important as producers. Diatoms store energy in the form of oil. Diatoms have silica in their cell walls. Brown Algae: Brown algae range from small forms with simple filaments to large multicellular algae. Some of the large brown algae, called kelps are tough and leathery, forms up to 75 metres in length, live in cooler marine water. The large brown kelps are leaflike in appearance. They possess leaflike blades, stemlike stipes and rootlike anchoring holdfasts. Brown algae also have chlorophyll (a and c) and carotenoids. Red Algae: They are mostly multicellular, present chiefly in warmer seawater growing in both shallow and deep waters. They can be up to a metre long attached to rocks or other substances by a basal holdfast. Red algae also have chlorophyll a and phycobilins. Green Algae: Green algae generally live in the ocean but are more likely found in freshwater and can even be found on land. Green algae have pigments (Chlorophyll a, b and carotenoid), energy storage products (starch) and cell wall composition (large part cellulose) similar to those of plants. Because of these and other features, it is generally accepted that plants and green algae share a common ancestry and monophyletic lineage (e.g., Chlamydomonas, Spirogyra, Volvox). Myxomycota and Oomycota: Fungi Like Protists The organisms of this category generally resemble with fungi in that they are non photosynthetic, heterotrophs and have bodies formed of thread like structures called hyphae. But these are not true fungi due to several reasons. Majority of them have centrioles. The cell wall is made up of cellulose unlike fungi. Therefore, they have been excluded from kingdom fungi. Two major groups of fungi like protists are Myxomycotes and Oomycotes or water molds. Slime molds: Slime molds are organisms that are fungus like in one phase of their life cycle and amoeba like in another phase of their life cycle. Slime molds are similar in some respects to fungi i.e., body is filamentous, saprotroph, and having nonmotile spores. Slime molds differ from fungi due to presence of motility in the life cycle. The body of slime molds is called plasmodium. It is a diploid multinucleated, cytoplasmic mass enveloped by slime sheath and is formed by the formation of zygote. The plasmodium can grow to 30 cm in diameter. They are found on damp, decaying logs and leaf litter. As the plasmodium creeps along, it ingest bacteria, yeast, cells and spores of fungi etc. Under certain conditions, the plasmodium is converted into numerous, stalked fruiting bodies, called sporangia that produce spores. Under favourable conditions, the spores germinate and release amoeboid cells or flagellated swarm cells, eventually two of them fuse to form a diploid zygote which develops into a multinucleated plasmodium once again.

The Water Molds: The water molds include white rusts and downy mildews. Most of the members of this group are parasites. Their body is called mycelium, composed of filamentous structures called hyphae as in fungi. The hyphae are aseptate (coenocytic), i.e., without cross walls (septa). Most oomycotes live in freshwater or saltwater or in soil. Asexual reproduction takes place by zoospores, which are motile and have two flagella. Zoospores are produced in sac like structure, the zoosporangium. For sexual reproduction there are two types of gametangia, female gametangium is called oogonium and the male gametangium is called antheridium. The flowing of the contents of antheridium into an oogonium leads to the individual fusion of one or more pairs of male nuclei with eggs. This produces a special kind of thick walled zygotic cell called an oospore. This structure gives the phylum its name, i.e., phylum oomycota, e.g., Phytophthora infestans. IMPORTANCE OF PROTISTS TO HUMANS A number of diseases in man are caused by protozoans such as, sleeping sickness, malaria and amoebic dysentery, which have already been discussed. Phytophthora infestans causes late blight in potatoes. Ecological role of protists The dinoflagellates and green algae are important sources of food and oxygen in freshwater and marine ecosystem and act as major producers in aquatic ecosystem. Some red algae incorporates calcium carbonate in their cell walls from sea water and help in building coral reefs along with coral animals. Dead foraminiferans sink to the bottom of ocean where their shells form a grey mud that is gradually transformed into chalk. Plankton provides food to organisms, but it is also harvested for human use. Diatomaceous earth can be used as a filtering agent or added to paints to give them a sparkling finish. Use of protists in genetic research and single cell protein (SCP) The plasmodial slime mold Physarum polycephalum has been used as an experimental organism that has been used to study many fundamental biological processes including growth and differentiation, cytoplasmic streaming, and the functions of cytoskeleton. Some protists are also used to produce single cell protein (SCP). GENERAL CHARACTERISTICS OF FUNGI The multicellular (except yeast), eukaryotic, absorptive heterotrophs which have cell wall made up of chitin and lack centrioles in their cells are classified as fungi. The study of fungi is called mycology. The person who studies fungi is called mycologist. Taxonomic status of fungi (Fungi as separate kingdom) Fungi are different from plants as: (1) Fungi have no chlorophyll (2) fungi never have flagella (3) fungi are saprotrophs. Fungi are different from animals as fungi: (i) have cell wall (ii) are absorptive heterotrophs (iii) are non-motile. So fungi can neither be placed in kingdom plantae nor in kingdom animalia. Similarly, fungi cannot be classified in kingdom Protista as fungi are not direct descendants of prokaryotes and they cannot be put into kingdom monera as fungi are eukaryotes. Fungi also show some unique characters not found in other kingdoms such as nuclear mitosis.

Because fungi are distinct from plants, animals and other eukaryotes in many ways, so they have been classified as separate kingdom. Habitat Fungi grow best in moist habitats, but are found wherever organic matter is present. They survive dry conditions in some resting stage or by producing resistant spores. They can also tolerate a wide range of pH from 2-9, a wide temperature range and high osmotic pressure such as in concentrated salt/sugar solutions as in jelly, jam etc. These features also help them in their survival on land. Cellular structure of fungi Fungal cells are eukaryotic in nature, have chitinous cell wall and lack centrioles and flagella. If carbohydrate is stored, it is usually as glycogen and not starch. Some cells have one nucleus (monokaryotic), some have two nuclei (dikaryotic) while other have multiple nuclei (multinucleate or coenocytic). Fungal cells show a unique mitotic division, called nuclear mitosis in which spindle fibers are formed within the nuclear envelope for the distribution of chromosomes to the daughter nuclei. Body structure of fungi The multicellular fungi form a network of filaments called hyphae. The entire mass of hyphae collectively is called mycelium. Mycelium may be monokaryotic or dikaryotic. The mycelium formed by fusion of two hyphae is called primary mycelium and that consists of dikaryotic cells is called secondary mycelium. The cross walls of septate hyphae are perforated allowing the cytoplasm to stream from one compartment to other. Yeasts are the only unicellular non hyphal fungi. Some fungi also form large fruiting bodies (basidiocarps and ascocarps) which are actually the clusters of reproductive structures. Locomotion in fungi Fungi are non-motile, lack basal bodies and do not have flagella at any stage of their life. They show chemotropism i.e., growth towards a food source. Modes of nutrition in fungi Fungi lack chlorophyll, so they are nonphotosynthetic. Thus, mode of nutrition is heterotrophic. Based upon ways of obtaining nutrient fungi may be saprotrophs, parasites, predators or symbionts (mutualists). Saprobic fungi: Most fungi are saprotrophs, decomposers that obtain their food directly from dead organic matter. They secrete out digestive enzymes, which digest dead organic matter and the small molecules thus produced are absorbed back into the fungus. Therefore, they are absorptive heterotrophs. Saprobic fungi anchor to the substrate by modified hyphae, the rhizoids. Parasitic fungi: Some fungi are parasites, some are even predators, and still others are mutualists. Parasitic fungi absorb nutrients directly from the living host cytoplasm with the help of specialized hyphae called haustoria. They may be obligate or facultative. Obligate parasites can live only on their host and cannot be grown on available defined growth culture medium. Powdery mildews and most rust species are obligate parasites. Facultative parasites can live on their host as well as by themselves on artificial growth media. Some fungi are active predators. The oyster mushroom (Pleurotus) is omnivorous. It paralyses the nematodes, penetrate them, and absorb their nutrients. It fulfills its glucose requirement by decomposing wood.

Another fungus Arthrobotrys forms constricting ring, dilates and captures soil nematodes. Symbiotic fungi: Lichen is a symbiotic relationship between a fungus (mostly an ascomycotes and a few basidiomycotes), and a green alga or a cyanobacterium. The body of lichen consists of three layers. Upper layer is thin and tough made up of closely packed fungal hyphae. The middle layer is also formed by fungal hyphae interwoven with photosynthetic cells. Bottom layer consists of loosely woven hyphae. Specialized fungal hyphae either penetrate or envelope the photosynthetic cells, transferring nutrients directly to the rest of the fungus. Mycorrhizae are mutualistic relationships between soil fungi and the roots of most plants. The hyphae help in the direct absorption of phosphorous, zinc, copper and other nutrients from the soil into the roots. Plants whose roots are invaded by mycorrhizae grow more successfully than do plants without mycorrhizae. There are two main types of mycorrhizae in which mycelia extend far out into the soil. Endomycorrhizae penetrate only into the outer cells of plant root forming coils, swellings and minute branches and also extend out into surrounding soil. Ectomycorrhizae form a covering that is exterior to the root, and they grow between cell walls. These are mostly formed with pines, firs etc. Reproduction in fungi The fungi reproduce both asexually and sexually. Asexual reproduction: It takes place by sporangiospore, conidiospore, budding and fragmentation. Sporangiospores are produced in spherical sac like structures, the sporangia which develop at the tip of special erectly growing hyphae, the sporangiophores e.g., Rhizopus. Conidiospores are produced in the form of a cluster of chains at the tip of erectly growing hyphae, the conidiophores e.g., Penicillium. Budding is a process in which first, nucleus is divided into two daughter nuclei by nuclear division, then a small outgrowth is formed which takes one of the daughter nuclei and subsequently gets separated from the parent cell. Fragmentation is the breakdown of mycelium into different fragments which again regenerate into new mycelium. Sexual reproduction: Life cycle for fungi. Fungi alternate between sexual and asexual reproductive stages. The mechanism of sexual reproduction vary in different groups of fungi but plasmogamy, karyogamy and meiosis are common to all. In sexual reproduction, hyphae of two different mating types fuse and undergo nuclear fusion (karyogamy). In two of the three main groups of fungi, there is a delay between plasmogamy and karyogamy. For a long period, hyphae with genetically different nuclei of two individuals may co-exist in the mycelium. Such a fungal hypha is called dikaryotic. CLASSIFICATION OF FUNGI The classification of fungi is based upon the way they produce sexual spores. Three main phyla of fungi are Zygomycota, Ascomycota and Basidiomycota. Zygomycota (Conjugating Fungi) The phylum zygomycota is called conjugating fungi because during sexual reproduction their hyphae are fused just like the conjugation in bacteria. They are mainly saprophytic. Hyphae are nonseptate, mycelium is well developed and haploid. Rhizoids for anchorage are found. Examples are Rhizopus and Mucor. Asexual reproduction takes place by non-motile spores produced in sporangium.

They are dispersed by wind. Sexual reproduction takes place when haploid hyphae of two different mating types designated as plus () and minus (-) come in contact. The tips of these hyphae swell and are cut off from the rest of the mycelium by the formation of septa. The tip cells are now called gametangia, structures that produce gametes. The gametangia fuse and their protoplasts mix. The plus and minus nuclei pair and then fuse to form a diploid nucleus, the zygote. There is no delay between plasmogamy and karyogamy and therefore, no dikaryotic phase. The zygote develops into a zygospore. The division or phylum name refers to the zygospore. Zygospores germinate under favourable conditions and divide by meiosis. The wall of the zygospore splits and hypha grows upward. The tip of the hypha develops into a sporangium. The sporangium contains many nuclei. The wall of the sporangium ruptures and spores are liberated. Each spore grows into a new plus or minus strain of mycelium. Ascomycota (Sac Fungi) Ascomycotes are the members of phylum ascomycota. It is a large group. Ascomycotes are also known as sac fungi because their sexual spores are produced in little sacs called asci. Their mycelium consist of septate hyphae. There is delay between plasmogamy and karyogamy. Therefore, both monokaryotic and dikaryotic phases are found in the life cycle. Asexual reproduction involves production of asexual spores called conidia or conidiospores. Conidia vary in shape, size and may be multicellular. The colour of conidia is what gives the characteristic green, blue, pink or other tint to many of these fungi. In unicellular yeasts, asexual reproduction takes place by budding and fission. Sexual reproduction takes place when two hyphae produced by the germination of haploid ascospores, grow together and their cytoplasm fused (plasmogamy). Within this common cytoplasm, haploid nuclei from the parent hyphae pair but do not fuse. New hyphae develop from the area of plasmogamy and the cells of these new hyphae are dikaryotic. The dikaryotic hyphae grow and form a fruiting body called ascocarp. A fruiting body is a cluster of many asci (singular ascus) intermixed with sterile hyphae. Within each ascus the two nuclei fuse and form a diploid nucleus, the zygote, which undergoes meiosis to form four haploid nuclei. This process is usually followed by one mitotic division of each of the four nuclei, resulting in eight haploid nuclei. Each haploid nucleus develops into an ascospore. The ascospores, are then windblown if they land on a suitable location and germinate to form a new primary mycelium of monokaryotic hyphae. The examples of sac fungi are Yeasts (Saccharomyces), Neurospora, Morels, Truffles, Penicillium. Basidiomycota (Club-Fungi) Basidiomycota includes edible and poisonous mushrooms, bracket fungi, puffballs and some notorious plant pathogens such as rust and smut. These fungi are commonly known as club fungi due to its characteristic club (rod) shaped reproductive structures, the basidia. These fungi also have primary and secondary septate mycelia of monokaryotic and dikaryotic hyphae respectively.

There is also a delay between plasmogamy and karyogamy during sexual reproduction. Although club fungi occasionally do produce conidiospores asexually, they usually reproduce sexually. Life cycle of a mushroom (Agaricus) The life cycle starts by the germination of characteristic haploid sexual spores of this fungus called basidiospores. Each basidiospore has the potential to give rise to a primary mycelium that consist of monokaryotic hyphae. The mycelium of Mushrooms consists of white, branched, thread like hyphae that occur mostly below ground. When the primary mycelium encounters another monokaryotic (n) hypha of opposite mating type, the two hyphae fuse. However the two haploid nuclei do not fuse and remain separate from each other. In this way a secondary mycelium with a dikaryotic (n n) hyphae is produced, in which each cell contains two haploid nuclei. The n n hyphae of the secondary mycelium grow and form compact mass, called buttons, along or just beneath the mycelium. Each button grows into a fruiting body known as mushroom. A mushroom, which consists of a stalk and a cap, is called basidiocarp. The lower surface of the cap usually consists of many thin perpendicular plates called gills of the mushroom. On the surface of these gills basidia are produced where haploid nuclei of the dikaryotic cells fuse to form diploid zygote. Meiosis then takes place forming four haploid nuclei that move into projections forming basidiospore, which are released later. IMPORTANCE OF FUNGI Fungi are useful to people in many ways but they are also harmful to human beings. Fungi cause economic gains as well as losses. Many scientists isolate different types of fungi and grow them to make various chemicals. Fungi cause diseases. Fungi cause diseases in animals and plants. Here we will discuss use of fungi, antibiotics obtained from fungi, edible fungi, ecological role of fungi and pathological role of fungi. Ecological impact of fungi Fungi make important contributions to the ecological balance of our world. Like bacteria, most fungi are saprotrophs, decomposers that digest and absorb nutrients from organic wastes and dead organisms. In this way fungi help in maintaining the nutrient balance. Fungi and bacteria are the major decomposers in nature. The organic waste is removed from the environment by the activity of saprotrophic fungi and bacteria. The fungi and bacteria liberate huge amounts of CO2 in the air by decomposing dead bodies of animals and plants. This carbon dioxide is used by green plants for the synthesis of organic food during photosynthesis. Thus fungi help in recycling of materials. Humus is an important constituent of soil and essential for the proper growth of plants. Humus is formed from the organic waste material by the activities of fungi and bacteria. Some fungi such as lichen also contribute in bioindication of pollution, reduction of environmental pollution and ecological succession (development of an ecosystem). Economic gains from Fungi Fungi are used as food, in baking, brewing and medicinal industries. Yeasts, Fungi are being used in genetic research as well.

Edible fungi: There are some 200 kinds of edible mushrooms e.g., Agaricus campestris, Agaricus bisporus etc. Some edible mushrooms are cultivated commercially. Truffles and morels produce underground fruiting bodies are also eaten. Aspergillus sp is used to produce soy sauce and soya paste from soya bean. Role of fungi in baking: Yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) is used in baking of bread. Yeast causes fermentation of sugar resulting in production of carbon dioxide gas. When making bread, the dough rises because of this gas. Role of fungi in brewing: The process of making alcohol by fermentation is called brewing. Different species of Saccharomyces (Yeast) are used in this process. Role of fungi in genetic research: Yeasts are used in the biological research, especially in genetic research. Researchers use Saccharomyces cerevisiae to study molecular genetics, because its cells are easy to grow and manipulate. Pink bread mold (Neurospora) has also been used for genetic research. Yeast was one of the first eukaryotes to be used in genetic engineering. In 1983, a functional artificial chromosome was made in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. It was also the first eukaryotes whose genome sequence was completely studied in 1996. Role of fungi in medicinal industry: The first antibiotic discovered was penicillin, made by the mold Penicillium notatum. Cyclosporine obtained from soil fungus is used in organ transplantation for preventing rejection. Griseofulvin obtained from Penicillium sp is used to inhibit fungal growth. Economic losses due to fungi Fungi are responsible for many important diseases in plants and also in animals including man. Plant diseases: Fungi are responsible for many serious plant diseases, including epidemics that often result in complete crop failure. All plants are susceptible to one or more kinds of fungal infection. Some important plant diseases caused by ascomycotes are powdery mildews, chestnut blight, Dutch elm disease, apple scab, and brown rot, which attack cherries, peaches, plums, and apricots. Diseases caused by basidiomycotes include smuts and rusts that attack various plants for example the cereal crops of corn, wheat, oats etc. Role of fungi in human diseases Some fungi cause superficial infections in which only the skin, hair, or nails are infected. Ringworm and athlete's foot are examples of fungal infection of the skin. Candidiasis is a yeast infection of mucous membrane of the mouth or vagina caused by Candida sp. Histoplasmosis is a serious infection of the lungs caused by inhaling spores of a soil fungus. Ergotism is caused by purple ergot rye. It causes nervous spasm, convulsion, psychotic delusion and even gangrene.

BIOLOGICAL MOLECULES 1 BIOLOGICAL MOLECULES IN PROTOPLASM Biological molecules are different chemical compounds of living beings. Biochemistry is the branch of biology that deals with such molecules. It also deals with various chemical reactions (metabolism) of living beings. 1 Chemical Composition of Protoplasm Approximately 25 elements out of 92 naturally occurring elements of earth are found in living beings. However, only 16 of these elements can be classified on the basis of their proportions in organisms. The six major bioelements constitute 99 of protoplasm. Minor elements are those that are found in small amounts, whereas those that are present in trace amounts are called trace elements. Major bioelements include oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, calcium and phosphorus. Minor elements include potassium and sulphur. Trace elements include iron, copper, manganese and zinc. Some trace elements such as iron are needed by all living beings, whereas others are needed only by certain species. Elements are combined with each other and can form thousands of different compounds. These may be inorganic (water and minerals) and organic (carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids). The proportions of these biomolecules are given in the table showing their distribution in bacterial and mammalian cells. The four fundamental kinds of biological molecules are carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. Carbohydrates are present in the cytoplasm of the cells and provide fuel for metabolic activities of the cell. Proteins are present in the membranes, ribosomes, secretory products and enzymes of the cell. Lipids are present in the membranes and cytoplasm of cells. Lipids provide a reserved energy source, shape, protect and insulate the cells. The nucleic acid DNA is present in the chromosome and controls the cell activity. RNA is present in the nucleoplasm and cytoplasm. It takes genetic information from DNA and helps in protein synthesis. Condensation and Hydrolysis Macromolecules are high molecular weight organic molecules which are made from many repeating units. These are also known as polymers. Monomers are micromolecules. The formation of polymers from monomers is carried out by condensation. When two monomers join, a water molecule is released. This process is also called dehydration synthesis. Hydrolysis is the reverse of condensation. It involves the breakdown of a polymer into monomers by the addition of water. Condensation reaction is repeated several times, resulting molecule will be a polymer. Condensation is also called dehydration synthesis. In this process, water is removed and a bond is formed. Hydrolysis is essentially the reverse of condensation. It involves the breakdown of a polymer into monomers by the addition of water. During hydrolysis, an OH group from water is attached to one monomer and H is attached to the other monomer. All digestion reactions are examples of hydrolysis which are controlled by enzymes such as carbohydrases, proteases, lipases and nucleases. 2 IMPORTANCE OF WATER Water is one of the main constituents on earth. More than two thirds of the earth is covered by water. Approximately 70 percent of any organism is formed of water.

The lowest percentage of water is found in seeds and bones (20) and the highest is in brain cells (8590). Jellyfish has exceptionally large amount of water i.e., 99. 1 Properties of Water that Make it the Cradle of Life The properties of water that make it the cradle of life are as follows: High polarity The bonds formed by the mutual sharing of electrons between two atoms are called covalent bonds. In the case of water, the sharing of electrons between oxygen and hydrogen is not equal, so the covalent bond is polar. Oxygen has a slight negative charge while hydrogen has a slight positive charge. Due to this polarity, water is an excellent solvent. Hydrogen Bonding The polarity of water molecules makes them interact with each other. The charged regions on each molecule are attracted to oppositely charged regions on neighbouring molecules, forming weak hydrogen bonds. These bonds give water high cohesion and adhesion. Cohesion and Adhesion Cohesion is the attraction among water molecules which enables them to stick together. Adhesion is the attraction of water molecules to other polar surfaces. These properties help water to act as a transport medium in living bodies. High Specific Heat Capacity Specific heat capacity is the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 g of a substance by 1C. Water has a high specific heat capacity due to hydrogen bonding. This allows water to stabilize temperature in organisms and environments. High Heat of Vaporization Heat of vaporization is the amount of heat required to convert a unit mass of liquid into vapour. Water has a high heat of vaporization. This property allows evaporation to cool organisms, such as sweating in animals. Hydrophobic Exclusion Hydrophobic exclusion is defined as the minimization of contact area between water and hydrophobic substances when they are placed in water. For example, oil droplets join together when placed in water. Biologically, hydrophobic exclusion plays a key role in maintaining the integrity of lipid bilayer membranes. Ionization The dissociation of a molecule into ions is called ionization. When water ionizes, it releases equal numbers of hydrogen ions (H) and hydroxyl ions (OH). This reaction is reversible and helps in maintaining pH in living systems. Lower Density of Ice Ice floats on water because it is less dense. Ice forms a lattice structure due to maximum hydrogen bonding, allowing aquatic organisms to survive beneath frozen surfaces. 3 CARBOHYDRATES Carbohydrates mean hydrates of carbon. They are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones or compounds that yield such units upon hydrolysis. 2 Biological Molecules Carbohydrates are organic compounds that are polyhydroxy aldehydes or polyhydroxy ketones, or can be converted into such compounds by chemical transformations such as oxidation or reduction. Classification of Carbohydrates Carbohydrates are commonly known as saccharides because most familiar carbohydrates have a sweet taste. Classification of carbohydrates is based upon the number of saccharide units. Carbohydrates are generally classified into three groups i.e., monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides. Fig.

2.9: Chemical nature of carbohydrates Table 2.2: Comparison of characteristics of carbohydrates Monosaccharides Oligosaccharides Polysaccharides They consist of a single saccharide unit. They are composed of 2 to 10 saccharide units. They are composed of more than 10 saccharide units. They are the simplest carbohydrates and cannot be further hydrolyzed. Upon hydrolysis they yield at least 2 and maximum 10 monosaccharides. Upon hydrolysis they yield at least 11 monosaccharides. Highly soluble in water. Less soluble in water. Generally insoluble in water. Sweetest among all carbohydrates. Less sweet in taste. Tasteless. Monosaccharides Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates. The number of carbon atoms in monosaccharides ranges from 3 to 7. All monosaccharides, except one carbon, have a hydroxyl group (OH) while one carbon atom is either part of an aldehyde or ketone group. The general empirical formula of monosaccharides is (CH₂O)ₙ, where n is the number of carbon atoms. Classification of monosaccharides is based upon functional group and number of carbon atoms. Those monosaccharides which contain aldehyde group are called aldoses, whereas those which contain ketone group are called ketoses. Functions of monosaccharides Erythrose: Intermediate in respiration. Ribose, Ribulose: Ribose and deoxyribose are components of RNA and DNA respectively. Ribulose is an intermediate in photosynthesis. Glucose, Fructose: Glucose is the primary respiratory fuel. Fructose is an intermediate in respiration. Galactose: Component of milk sugar. Glucoheptose / Sedoheptulose: Intermediates in photosynthesis. Chemical structure of monosaccharides Monosaccharides are usually found in open-chain structure in crystalline form, but when dissolved in water most pentoses and hexoses are converted into ring-chain structure. Let us understand this by taking ribose (C₅H₁₀O₅) as an example. Ribose exists in open-chain structure in dried form but in aqueous medium it exists in ring structure. When dissolved in water, the oxygen atom from aldehyde group reacts with the hydroxyl group of C₄ forming a ring. Thus oxygen links C₁ and C₄ and the OH group shifts accordingly. Fig. 2.12: α and β isomers of glucose Each pentose or hexose molecule in ring structure exists in either α or β form depending upon the position of H and OH group on C₁. If OH group is downward on C₁, it is called α-sugar; if OH is upward, it is called β-sugar. Isomers of glucose Isomers have the same molecular formula but differ in spatial arrangement. Enantiomers are stereoisomers that are mirror images of each other but cannot be superimposed. These mirror images are identical in shape but cannot be placed on top of each other. An example is right-handed and left-handed molecules. Artificial (Laboratory Manufactured) Sweeteners Laboratory manufactured sugars are L-sugars. Naturally occurring sugars in living organisms are D-sugars. Enzymes and cell receptors are designed to react only with D-sugars. Therefore, left-handed sugars cannot be recognized by right-handed enzymes. Just like a glove fits only on the proper hand, an enzyme cannot react with a substrate of opposite configuration. Fig. 2.13: Example of enantiomers Oligosaccharides Oligosaccharides are carbohydrates formed by condensation of 210 monosaccharide units.

Based on the number of monosaccharide units, they are classified into disaccharides, trisaccharides, etc. The most common are disaccharides. Disaccharides are less sweet in taste and less soluble in water. They can be hydrolyzed into monosaccharides. The general formula of common disaccharides is C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁. Examples include sucrose, maltose, and lactose. Sucrose Sucrose is commonly known as cane sugar. It is widely distributed in plants and is the main transport disaccharide. It is highly soluble in water and chemically unreactive. It is formed by condensation of glucose and fructose through α-1,2-glycosidic linkage. Maltose Maltose is known as malt sugar. It is an intermediate product in the digestion of starch and glycogen. Maltose is formed by condensation of two α-glucose molecules through α-1,4-glycosidic linkage. Fig. 2.15: Formation of maltose Lactose Lactose is commonly known as milk sugar. It is formed by condensation of β-galactose and β-glucose through β-1,4-glycosidic linkage. Fig. 2.16: Formation of lactose Reducing and Non-reducing Sugars Carbohydrates capable of being oxidized and reducing other substances are called reducing sugars. All monosaccharides and maltose and lactose are reducing sugars. Sucrose and polysaccharides are non-reducing sugars. Polysaccharides Polysaccharides are carbohydrates which upon hydrolysis yield more than ten monosaccharide units. They are the largest group of carbohydrates. Polysaccharides formed from only one type of monosaccharide are called homopolysaccharides, e.g., starch, glycogen, cellulose, chitin. Polysaccharides formed from different monosaccharides are called heteropolysaccharides, e.g., pectin and peptidoglycan. Because of their large size, polysaccharides are ideal storage molecules. They do not dissolve in water and hence do not exert osmotic pressure. They can be easily converted into monosaccharides by hydrolysis when required. Starch Starch is a homopolysaccharide composed of hundreds of glucose units. It is the storage carbohydrate of plants and is mainly stored in seeds, fruits, and tubers. Starch digestion begins in the mouth and small intestine by amylase enzyme, yielding maltose which is further digested by maltase. Starch gives blue color with iodine solution. There are two types of starch: amylose and amylopectin. Fig. 2.17: Structure of starch Glycogen Glycogen is a homopolysaccharide similar to amylopectin starch but has much more branching. It is formed by α-1,4-glycosidic linkages with α-1,6-glycosidic branching. Glycogen is the storage carbohydrate of animals and is mainly stored in liver and muscles. It gives red color with iodine solution. Cellulose Cellulose is the most abundant carbohydrate on earth. It is a homopolysaccharide composed of hundreds of β-glucose molecules. It is the main structural component of plant cell walls. Cotton and paper are nearly pure forms of cellulose. Fig. 2.19: Structure of cellulose Cellulose does not give any color with iodine solution. Its structure resembles amylose starch in being unbranched, but it differs in having β-1,4-glycosidic linkages between glucose units. Science Tidbits Cellulose cannot be digested by humans, but it must be taken in diet as roughage. It prevents abnormal absorption of food in intestine. Herbivores possess symbiotic microorganisms that secrete cellulase enzyme to digest cellulose. Upon hydrolysis, cellulose first yields cellobiose, which is further digested into glucose.

Chitin Chitin is the second most abundant organic molecule on earth. It is a structural homopolysaccharide found in fungal cell walls and exoskeleton of arthropods. Due to its presence in fungi, it is also called fungal cellulose. Chitin is made of N-acetyl glucosamine monomers linked by β-1,4-glycosidic bonds. Fig. 2.20: Structure of chitin Proteins Proteins are the main structural components of cells. All proteins contain carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen; some also contain sulfur. A few proteins contain iron, iodine or magnesium. Structure of Proteins Proteins are polymers of amino acids. They may consist of a single polypeptide chain or more than one polypeptide chain. Amino Acids Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. Only 20 amino acids are commonly found in proteins. Each amino acid contains a central carbon atom to which a hydrogen atom, an amino group (NH₂), a carboxyl group (COOH) and a variable side chain (R group) are attached. Fig. 2.21: General structure of an amino acid The R group differs in each amino acid and determines its chemical properties. Dipeptides and Polypeptides Amino acids join together by condensation reactions during protein synthesis on ribosomes. During this reaction, OH from carboxyl group and H from amino group are released forming a water molecule, and a peptide bond is formed. Fig. 2.22: Formation of dipeptide and peptide bond The end containing free amino group is called N-terminal end, while the end containing free carboxyl group is called C-terminal end. When three amino acids join, a tripeptide is formed. When many amino acids join through peptide bonds, a polypeptide chain is formed. Levels of Protein Organization Primary Structure It is the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain. Secondary Structure It occurs when the polypeptide chain coils or folds due to hydrogen bonding, forming alpha-helix or beta-pleated sheet structures. Tertiary Structure It occurs due to interactions between side chains including hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, and disulfide bridges, resulting in a globular shape. Quaternary Structure It is formed when more than one polypeptide chain associates to form a functional protein. Fig. 2.23: Structural conformations in proteins Significance of Amino Acid Sequence The sequence of amino acids determines protein function. A change in even a single amino acid may alter protein function. Sickle Cell Anemia Normal red blood cells are disc-shaped and flexible. Hemoglobin contains four polypeptide chains: two alpha chains (141 amino acids each) and two beta chains (146 amino acids each). Sickle cell anemia is caused by a point mutation in the beta-globin gene. In this disorder, glutamic acid is replaced by valine at the sixth position of beta chain, producing sickle hemoglobin (HbS). This causes red blood cells to become sickle-shaped and sticky, leading to blockage of blood vessels. Fig. 2.24: Difference in beta-chain of HbA and HbS Classification of Proteins Based on structure and shape, proteins are classified into: Fibrous Proteins These proteins have fiber-like shape, are insoluble in water and provide structural support. Examples include collagen, keratin, actin, myosin, elastin and fibrin.

Globular Proteins These proteins are spherical in shape, soluble in water and perform functional roles. Examples include enzymes, hormones, antibodies and transport proteins. Roles of Proteins Structural Proteins Collagen forms bone and cartilage matrix Elastin supports connective tissues Keratin forms hair, nails, feathers and horns Histones organize DNA into chromosomes Functional Proteins Enzymes regulate metabolism Hormones regulate physiological processes Antibodies provide immunity Hemoglobin transports oxygen Fibrinogen helps in blood clotting 2 Biological Molecules Fatty acids are of two types i.e., saturated and unsaturated fatty acids. Saturated fatty acids contain no double bonds between carbon atoms and are fully saturated with hydrogen, e.g., palmitic acid and stearic acid. Saturated fatty acids are solid at room temperature and are common in animal fats. Unsaturated fatty acids contain one or more pairs of carbon atoms joined by a double bond and are not fully saturated with hydrogen, e.g., oleic acid. Unsaturated fatty acids are liquid at room temperature, have lower melting point and are more common in plant lipids. Triacylglycerols containing unsaturated hydrocarbon chains melt at a lower temperature. This property is useful for maintaining membrane fluidity. Waxes Waxes are highly hydrophobic compounds. There are two types of waxes: Natural waxes are simple lipids. They are typically esters of long-chain fatty acids and long-chain alcohols, such as beeswax (found in honeycomb) and cutin (present on leaf surfaces of plants). These waxes are chemically inert and resistant to atmospheric oxidation. Waxes perform protective functions in plants and animals. Synthetic waxes are generally derived from petroleum or polyethylene, for example paraffin wax, which is used to make candles. Phospholipids Phospholipids are derived from phosphatidic acid. A phospholipid is formed when phosphatidic acid combines with one of the four organic compounds such as choline (a nitrogenous base), ethanolamine (an amino alcohol), inositol (a cyclic alcohol) and serine (an amino acid). A phosphatidic acid molecule is similar to diglyceride but contains a glycerol molecule, two fatty acids esterified with the first and second hydroxyl groups of glycerol, and a phosphate group esterified with the third hydroxyl group. The most common phospholipid is phosphatidylcholine, also known as lecithin, in which choline is attached to the phosphate group of phosphatidic acid. Fig. 2.27: Phosphatidylcholine One end of the phospholipid molecule containing the phosphate group and additional compound is polar and readily soluble in water, whereas the other end containing fatty acid chains is non-polar and insoluble in water. Therefore, phospholipids are amphipathic molecules and are the main components of cell membranes. Terpenes Terpenes are synthesized from a five-carbon building block known as isoprene unit. These isoprene units condense in different ways to form many compounds. Two isoprene units form a monoterpene, e.g., menthol; four isoprene units form a diterpene, e.g., phytol (tail of chlorophyll); many isoprene units form polyterpenes, e.g., natural rubber. Steroids Steroids are lipids of high molecular weight which can be crystalline. A steroid consists of 17 carbon atoms arranged in four attached rings.

Three of these rings contain six carbon atoms each, while the fourth ring contains five carbon atoms. The length and structure of side chains extending from these rings distinguish one steroid from another. These structures are synthesized from isoprene units. Cholesterol is an important steroid and is a structural component of cell membranes. Cholesterol is the precursor of many biologically important steroids such as bile acids, male sex hormone testosterone, female sex hormones progesterone and estrogen. Bile salts, which emulsify fats, and vitamin D, which helps regulate calcium metabolism, are also derived from cholesterol. Fig. 2.29: Steroid nucleus Prostaglandins Prostaglandins are found in almost every mammalian tissue and act as local hormones. They are derived from arachidonic acid. Their functions vary depending on tissue type. Some prostaglandins lower blood pressure, whereas others raise it. In the immune system, prostaglandins help induce fever and inflammation and intensify the sensation of pain. They also cause aggregation of platelets, an early step in blood clot formation. The ability of aspirin to reduce fever and pain depends on inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis. Society Connections The changes associated with inflammation are characterized by redness (rubor), heat (calor), swelling (tumor) and pain (dolor). These changes are due to dilation of local blood vessels and increased permeability, allowing white blood cells to move into the inflamed tissues.
