This compound was neither a lipid nor a carbohydrate; therefore, it was a novel type of biological molecule. He named this molecule nuclein because it was located in the nucleus. The basic structure and chemical nature of nuclein were determined in 1920 and it was renamed nucleic acid due to its acidic nature. Chemical Structure of Nucleic Acids It is now clear that nucleic acids are of two types, i.e., deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and ribonucleic acid (RNA). Both nucleic acids are linear, unbranched polymers. The monomers of nucleic acids are called nucleotides. Composition of a Nucleotide Nucleotides of DNA are called deoxyribonucleotides and those of RNA are called ribonucleotides. Each nucleotide consists of three components: A pentose sugar A phosphate group A nitrogen-containing base The pentose sugar in deoxyribonucleotides is deoxyribose, while in ribonucleotides it is ribose. Nitrogenous bases are of two types: Pyrimidines: cytosine (C), thymine (T) and uracil (U) Purines: adenine (A) and guanine (G) Thymine is found only in DNA, whereas uracil is found only in RNA. A nucleoside consists of a pentose sugar and a nitrogenous base. When a phosphate group is attached to the 5 carbon of the sugar, the molecule is called a nucleotide. If one phosphate group is attached, it is called a nucleoside monophosphate; with two phosphate groups, it is called a nucleoside diphosphate; and with three phosphate groups, it is called a nucleoside triphosphate. Polymerization of Nucleotides (Formation of Polynucleotide) Nucleotides are joined together by condensation reactions.

Unlike proteins, carbohydrates and lipids, the molecule released during this reaction is not water but pyrophosphate (two phosphate groups bound together). When pyrophosphate is cleaved by the addition of water, a large amount of free energy is released. This energy is used to form phosphodiester bonds, linking nucleotides into a polymer called a polynucleotide. Polynucleotide chains have a free 5 phosphate group at one end and a free 3 hydroxyl group at the other end. By convention, nucleotide sequences are written in the 5 to 3 direction. Fig. 2.32: Polymerization of nucleotides Structure and Role of ATP Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) is a nucleotide composed of: Adenine (a nitrogenous base) Ribose (a pentose sugar) Three phosphate groups ATP contains high-energy covalent bonds linking the phosphate groups. ATP can be converted into adenosine diphosphate (ADP) or adenosine monophosphate (AMP) by the removal of phosphate groups, releasing energy that is used for cellular activities. Formation of Polynucleotide Chains Nucleotides are joined together by condensation reactions. In contrast to proteins, carbohydrates and lipids, the molecule released during this reaction is not water but pyrophosphate (two phosphate groups bound together). When pyrophosphate is cleaved by the addition of water, a large amount of free energy is released. This released energy is used to form phosphodiester bonds between nucleotides, resulting in the formation of a polynucleotide chain. Polynucleotide chains possess a free 5 phosphate group at one end and a free 3 hydroxyl group at the other end. By convention, nucleotide sequences are written in the 5 3 direction. ATP contains high-energy covalent bonds linking the phosphate groups. ATP can be converted into adenosine diphosphate (ADP) or adenosine monophosphate (AMP) by removal of phosphate groups, releasing energy required for cellular activities. Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) is another important nucleotide. It consists of two nucleotides joined by their phosphate groups forming a dinucleotide. One nucleotide contains adenine, ribose and phosphate, while the other contains nicotinamide, ribose and phosphate. NAD functions as a coenzyme in oxidationreduction reactions. Fig. 2.34: Structure of NAD Watson and Crick Model of DNA In 1951, Erwin Chargaff discovered that the nitrogenous bases in DNA show specific ratios. He observed that the amount of adenine is always equal to the amount of thymine, and the amount of guanine is always equal to the amount of cytosine. This observation is known as Chargaffs rule, which states that total purines are equal to total pyrimidines in DNA. During the same period, X-ray diffraction analysis of DNA was carried out by Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin, who suggested that DNA has a double helical structure. In 1953, based on these findings, James Watson and Francis Crick proposed the physical model of DNA, now known as the Watson and Crick model of DNA.

According to this model, DNA is composed of two polynucleotide chains that are held together by specific base pairing. The two chains run in opposite directions, i.e., one strand runs from 5 to 3 and the other from 3 to 5, making them antiparallel. Adenine pairs with thymine by two hydrogen bonds, while guanine pairs with cytosine by three hydrogen bonds. The width of the DNA double helix is 2 nm. Each complete turn of the helix is 3.4 nm long and consists of 10 base pairs. Fig. 2.35: WatsonCrick model of DNA PAGE 55 (CLEANED FULL, UNCUT) The two polynucleotide chains of DNA are coiled around each other to form a double helix. The chains are antiparallel, meaning one chain runs in the 5 to 3 direction while the other runs in the 3 to 5 direction. The base pairing is highly specific: adenine pairs only with thymine, and guanine pairs only with cytosine. There are two hydrogen bonds between adenine and thymine, while three hydrogen bonds exist between guanine and cytosine. These hydrogen bonds hold the two strands together. Each turn of the DNA helix contains ten base pairs. The sequence of nucleotides along the DNA strand can vary and is specific for different species, organisms, and even individuals. Science Titbits Watson and Crick proposed the molecular model of DNA and published their two-page article in the journal Nature in April 1953. This discovery had a profound impact on biology. Watson, Crick, and Maurice Wilkins were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1962 for their contribution to understanding the structure of DNA. Concept of Gene A gene is a specific region of DNA composed of a sequence of nucleotides. It is the physical and functional unit of heredity. Each gene contains information required to synthesize a specific protein. Genes determine individual characteristics such as eye color, hair color, and other inherited traits. To produce proteins, genetic information from DNA is copied into messenger RNA (mRNA). The mRNA then moves from the nucleus to the ribosomes, where it directs the synthesis of a specific polypeptide that folds into a functional protein. Ribonucleic Acid (RNA) RNA is a polymer of nucleotides similar to DNA, but it is generally single-stranded and does not form a double helix. However, some regions of RNA may form secondary double-stranded structures due to complementary base pairing. There are three major types of RNA, each transcribed from DNA and involved in protein synthesis: Messenger RNA (mRNA) mRNA consists of a single strand of variable length, depending on the size of the protein it codes for. For example, a protein composed of 100 amino acids requires an mRNA molecule containing 300 nucleotides. Each group of three nucleotides on mRNA is called a codon, which codes for a specific amino acid. mRNA carries the genetic message from DNA in the nucleus to the ribosomes in the cytoplasm, where protein synthesis occurs. Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) rRNA is transcribed from genes present on several chromosomes.

It combines with proteins to form ribosomes. Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis. rRNA constitutes approximately 80 of the total RNA content of a cell. It provides a structural platform on which protein synthesis takes place. Transfer RNA (tRNA) tRNA is the smallest RNA molecule and consists of about 75 to 90 nucleotides. It is single-stranded but folds into a characteristic cloverleaf shape due to internal base pairing. The 5 end of tRNA terminates with guanine, while the 3 end always ends with the sequence CCA, where an amino acid attaches. Each tRNA has an anticodon loop containing three nucleotides that are complementary to the codon on mRNA. Fig. 2.36: Cloverleaf model of tRNA Each tRNA molecule carries a specific amino acid from the cytoplasm to the ribosome during protein synthesis. There is at least one specific tRNA for each of the 20 amino acids found in proteins. In human cells, about 45 different tRNA molecules have been identified. 7 CONJUGATED MOLECULES Molecules formed by the combination of two different types of biomolecules are called conjugated molecules. Common conjugated molecules include glycolipids, glycoproteins, lipoproteins, and nucleoproteins. Glycolipids Glycolipids are complex lipids formed by the combination of lipids and carbohydrates. They are present in the white matter of the brain, myelin sheath of nerve fibers, and chloroplast membranes. Glycoproteins Glycoproteins are formed when proteins are covalently attached to carbohydrates. They are widely distributed in cells and function as hormones, transport proteins, and receptors. Blood group antigens are glycoproteins and play an important role in blood grouping. Lipoproteins Lipoproteins are complexes of proteins and lipids. They are found in blood plasma, cell membranes, egg yolk, milk, and chloroplasts of plants. They are involved in lipid transport. Nucleoproteins Nucleoproteins consist of nucleic acids and simple basic proteins. They are found in chromosomes and ribosomes. Career in Biochemistry Biochemistry is the study of chemical processes occurring in living organisms. It is a broad field offering a wide range of career opportunities. Biochemists may work in medical research, genetics, pharmacology, immunology, bioinformatics, forensic science, toxicology, food science, and agriculture. The applications of biochemistry continue to expand with scientific advancement.

CELL STRUCTURE AND FUNCTIONS All organisms are familiar with the word cell, i.e., a basic unit of life. By the middle of the nineteenth century, biologists had formulated cell theory which is a fundamental concept of biology. The generally accepted portions of the modern cell theory are as follows: (i) The cell is the fundamental unit of structure and function in living things. (ii) All organisms are made up of one or more cells. (iii) Cells arise from other cells through cellular division. This chapter will help you to become familiar with the structure of cells and how they work, and also the basic techniques essential for cell study. 1 TECHNIQUES USED IN CELL BIOLOGY To know the structure and functions of cells and cell organelles, some of the techniques will be discussed here in brief. 1 Cell Fractionation Cell fractionation is the combination of various methods used to separate cell organelles and components based upon size and density. It is very useful for electron microscopy of cell components. The principle of cell fractionation consists of two steps, i.e., homogenization and centrifugation. Homogenization It is the formation of a homogeneous mass of cells. It involves the grinding of cells in a suitable medium with correct pH, ionic composition and temperature. In plants, enzyme pectinase is added to digest middle lamella. This can be done in a blender. This procedure gives rise to a uniform mixture of cells which is then centrifuged. Centrifugation Centrifugation is the process to separate substances on the basis of their size and densities under the influence of centrifugal force. It is done by the machine called centrifuge. This machine can spin the tubes at very high speed. Spinning the tubes exerts a centrifugal force on the contents. There are two major ways of centrifugation, i.e., density gradient centrifugation and differential centrifugation. In density gradient centrifugation, the cell components of different sizes and densities are separated in different layers. The upper layers are less dense than the lower layers. In differential centrifugation, the size and shape of particles determine how fast it settles. A series of increasing speeds can be used. At each step, the contents which settle at the bottom of the tube are called pellet and those that remain suspended above in the form of liquid are called supernatant. After each speed, the supernatant can be drawn off and centrifuged again. A series of pellets containing cell organelles of smaller and smaller size can therefore be obtained. Bigger particles sediment faster and have higher sedimentation coefficients (Svedberg units). Sedimentation coefficients are, however, not additive. Sedimentation rate depends on the shape and volume of a particle, and when two particles bind together there is an increase in sedimentation. Thus, when measured separately they will have Svedberg values that may not add up in the compound particle. This is notably the case with the ribosome. Ribosomes are most often identified by their sedimentation coefficient.

For instance, the 70S ribosome that comes from bacteria has an actual sedimentation coefficient of 70 Svedberg, although it is composed of a 50S subunit and a 30S subunit. 2 Differential Staining Most biological structures are transparent. In order to differentiate between these structures, various coloured dyes are applied. Such techniques are called staining techniques. When only one stain, such as borax carmine (that stains nucleus), is used, it is called single staining. When two stains, one that will stain nucleus (e.g., haematoxylin) and other that will stain cytoplasm (e.g., eosin), are used, the process is called double staining or differential staining. 3 Microdissections Microdissection refers to the variety of techniques where a microscope is used to assist in dissection. It is generally used to remove tumour or granules from delicate tissues or cells like brain, heart and nerve cells. In this technique, the image is seen on a large TV screen or monitor while dissecting. 4 Tissue Culture Growth of a cell or a tissue on a chemical medium under controlled conditions is called tissue culture. This technique can be employed for plants and animals. Plant tissue culturing is mainly used for plant cloning, i.e., production of identical plants (clones). Animal tissue culture is usually set up by growing individual cells over the surface of a glass container. Animal tissue cultures are used to sense any abnormality in the cell, e.g., cancer, chromosomal disorder, etc. 5 Chromatography Chromatography is a technique which is used to separate different chemical compounds from a mixture. It is generally used for the separation of mixtures of proteins, amino acids or photosynthetic pigments. There are different types of chromatographic techniques. Paper chromatography is a simple and most widely used technique. It involves two phases: stationary phase, which is cellulose filter paper, and mobile phase, which is solvent in which sample mixture is dissolved. When the solvent travels over the paper, the mixture sample begins to separate and appears as dots at different places on paper according to their affinity. This paper is then called chromatogram. Below is the cleaned and corrected continuation, keeping content, length, and meaning intact. 6 Electrophoresis Electrophoresis is a technique which is used to separate charged polymer molecules on the basis of their size, shape, molecular weight and surface charge whether positive () or negative (). Such charged polymer molecules include DNA, RNA and proteins. This technique utilizes a gel medium for the separation of fragments which is done under the influence of an electric field.

Often the gel is sandwiched between glass or plastic plates to form a viscous slab. The two ends of the slab are suspended in two salt solutions that are connected by electrodes to a power source. At one end of the slab the samples are loaded. When voltage is applied to the apparatus, the molecules present in the gel migrate through the electric field. The negatively charged molecules move towards the positive pole and the positively charged molecules move towards the negative pole. The velocity of movement of fragments is inversely proportional to the size. Therefore, smaller fragments move faster than larger ones. In this way all the fragments are separated in the gel after some time. Later on the molecules can be pinpointed by staining the gel. 7 Spectrophotometry Spectrophotometry is a technique which is used to determine the absorption of different wavelengths of light by a particular chemical compound or a photosynthetic pigment. For this purpose, the instrument used is called spectrophotometer. The amount of light absorbed at each wavelength is plotted in a graph called the absorption spectrum. Spectrophotometry can be used to determine the wavelengths of light that take part in photosynthesis. It can also be used to determine the very minute quantity of a substance. 8 Resolution and Magnification in Microscopy The minimum capacity of a lens to differentiate between two adjacent points is called resolution. The resolution of the naked eye is 0.1 mm. This resolution can be increased by increasing magnification. Magnification is the capacity of an optical instrument to increase the size of an object more than its original size. The objects which cannot be seen by the naked eye can also be observed by increasing magnification. Different lenses have different magnification powers which are represented by the letter X, meaning the number of times larger than the original size. Therefore, a lens of 10X magnification power can increase the size of an object from 4 µm to 40 µm. Electron microscopy is the technique used to visualize objects that cannot be seen by the naked eye or light microscope. A common compound microscope consists of ocular and objective lenses. The magnification power of such a microscope is equal to the product of magnification powers of both lenses. The resolving power of a light microscope is 250 nm and its magnification is up to 4000X. The resolving power of an electron microscope is 0.2 nm and its magnification is up to 2,000,000X. 9 Micrometry Micrometry is the measurement of the size of objects under a microscope. It involves the use of two micrometers. The ocular micrometer is a glass disc with 100 equal divisions with no absolute value. It is placed in the eyepiece of the microscope. Then it is calibrated by using a stage micrometer. The stage micrometer is a glass slide with an exact scale like a miniature transparent ruler.

By superimposing the images of the ocular micrometer and stage micrometer scales, it is calibrated so that the size of any given object viewed under the microscope can be estimated. 2 CELL WALL AND PLASMA MEMBRANE The plasma membrane is the outer living boundary of the cell. Many cells have an extracellular component that is formed exterior to the membrane, which is called the cell wall. 1 Cell Wall The cell wall is present in plant cells, prokaryotes and fungi, but animal cells do not have a cell wall. This is probably due to their locomotor mode of life. Plant cell walls made up of cellulose differ in chemical composition from those of prokaryotes made up of peptidoglycan and fungi made up of chitin. The cell wall is secreted by the cell. It is porous and allows free passage of water and dissolved materials. The plant cell wall consists of three main layers: primary cell wall, middle lamella and secondary cell wall. Primary Cell Wall The primary cell wall is a true wall and develops in newly growing cells, i.e., during cell growth. It is present inner to the middle lamella. The primary cell wall is thin and slightly flexible. The primary cell wall is mainly composed of cellulose microfibrils embedded in a matrix of polysaccharides like hemicelluloses and pectin. The microfibrils are arranged in layers one above the other. This feature allows the wall to stretch plastically and reversibly. Therefore, the primary cell wall is adapted to growth. Secondary Cell Wall The secondary cell wall is formed between the primary cell wall and plasma membrane only in sclerenchyma cells. The plant cells possessing secondary cell wall are generally dead and provide mechanical support to the plant. The secondary cell wall is formed when the cell has reached its maximum growth because it is very rigid and does not allow further growth. The secondary cell wall contains lignin, inorganic salts and waxes. Lignin cements and anchors cellulose microfibrils together and provides rigidity to the cell. The secondary cell wall gives strength to the cell and provides definite shape. Middle Lamella Middle lamella is a sticky, gel-like layer present between adjacent cells which holds them together. It is composed mainly of pectic acids, calcium and magnesium salts. 2 Plasma Membrane The plasma membrane is also called plasmalemma. It is present in all living cells including prokaryotes. It controls the movement of materials into and out of the cell. 3 Fluid Mosaic Model of Plasma Membrane The fluid mosaic model of plasma membrane proposes that the membrane consists of a phospholipid bilayer in which protein molecules are either partially or wholly embedded. The phospholipids form a bilayer in which hydrophobic ends face each other while hydrophilic ends face outward. Proteins are scattered throughout the membrane in an irregular pattern just like large icebergs floating in the sea. The pattern of distribution of proteins can vary from membrane to membrane and also vary on both surfaces of the membrane.

The membrane is about 7 nm thick. The lipid part of plasma membrane consists of two layers of phospholipids. Steroids such as cholesterol are wedged into the phospholipid bilayer at some intervals. The plasma membrane is asymmetrical, i.e., its two surfaces are not identical. In general, most membrane proteins drift sideways in the fluid bilayer. The proteins within the membrane determine most of the membrane functions. Carbohydrates are attached either to proteins (glycoproteins) or lipids (glycolipids) and are generally present on the outer surface of the membrane. Filaments of the cytoskeleton are also present on the inner surface of the membrane which support the plasma membrane. Functions of Plasma Membrane Lipids The lipid part of the plasma membrane controls the fluidity of the membrane. When the concentration of unsaturated fatty acids in phospholipids increases, the bilayer becomes more fluid and the membrane becomes more flexible. Cholesterol helps to stabilize the lipid bilayer and restricts the entry and exit of polar molecules and ions. Functions of Plasma Membrane Proteins A variety of proteins are found in plasma membrane which may act as transport proteins, enzymes, receptors or antigens. Carrier Proteins Some plasma membrane proteins act as carrier proteins. Some of these have a channel through the membrane, while others bind the substance and help it to move across the membrane. Enzymes Some plasma membrane proteins have enzymatic functions, e.g., adenylate cyclase which converts ATP to cyclic AMP (cAMP). Receptor Molecules Some proteins in the plasma membrane act as receptors and receive signals from other cells. Each type of receptor has a specific shape. Binding of a molecule to a receptor can bring about an intracellular response. For example, hormones circulate in the blood but bind to specific target cells with specific receptors. Antigens Some proteins are antigens which enable the cells to recognize other cells. Foreign antigens can be recognized and attacked by the immune system. Role of Glycolipids and Glycoproteins as Cell Surface Markers Mostly glycolipids and glycoproteins act as cell surface markers. They are involved in cell-to-cell recognition and sticking the correct cells together in tissues. Regulation of Cells Interaction with its Environment The plasma membrane regulates cells interaction with its environment by controlling transport of materials across the cell. Transport across plasma membrane occurs to obtain nutrients, excrete waste substances, secrete useful substances, generate ionic gradients essential for nervous and muscular activity, and maintain a suitable pH and ionic concentration within the cell for enzyme activity. 3 CYTOPLASM AND CELL ORGANELLES The living matter of a cell is called protoplasm. In eukaryotic cells it can be divided into two parts, i.e., cytoplasm and nucleus. Cytoplasm Cytoplasm is the region between nuclear membrane and plasma membrane. It is present in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. The major difference between these two kinds of cells is the presence or absence of cytoskeleton and membrane-bound organelles. These structures are absent in prokaryotic cells. Chemical Nature of Cytoplasm Cytoplasm contains water and forms a solution that contains all the fundamental biomolecules.

Some of these are ions and small molecules such as sugars, amino acids, fatty acids, nucleotides and vitamins which remain in true solution. Others like proteins form colloidal solutions. The inner portion of cytoplasm is called cytosol while the peripheral region is more viscous and is called ectoplasm. Cyclosis The movement of cytoplasm is called cyclosis which is responsible for the distribution of cell organelles. Metabolic and Storage Role of Cytoplasm The cytoplasm acts as a site of metabolism and storehouse of the cell. Metabolic reactions generally occur in the cytosol which include protein synthesis and glycolysis. The cytoplasm is also concerned with storage of useful compounds which are subsequently used in cellular activities and waste compounds which are eliminated from the cell from time to time. 4 Cell Organelles In a eukaryotic cell, the cytoplasm contains highly organized discrete structures which are specific for various cellular functions and are called cell organelles. The cell organelles are generally enclosed by membranes except a few such as ribosomes. The organelles present in the cytoplasmic matrix of a cell are endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes, Golgi complex, lysosomes, peroxysomes, glyoxysomes, vacuoles, mitochondria and chloroplasts. Endoplasmic Reticulum Endoplasmic reticulum is an interconnecting network of tubules and cisternae which is generally extended from nuclear membrane to the plasma membrane throughout the cytoplasm of all eukaryotic cells. There are two types of endoplasmic reticulum, rough ER and smooth ER. Most cells contain both types of ER. However, some cells like skeletal muscle cells have more smooth ER, where it is called sarcoplasmic reticulum. Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum Rough ER has ribosomes attached on the sides facing the cytoplasm and has a rough appearance under electron microscope. Rough ER is mainly concerned with protein synthesis due to the association of ribosomes. It also provides mechanical support to the cell. Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum Smooth ER is continuous with rough ER. Since ribosomes are not attached to it, it has a smooth appearance under electron microscope. Smooth ER functions in metabolic processes such as metabolism of carbohydrates, detoxification of drugs especially in liver cells, and synthesis of lipids including oils, phospholipids and steroids. Smooth ER also stores calcium ions which are released during muscle contraction. It also transports various cellular products within the cell. PAGE 19 Golgi Complex The Golgi complex is found in all eukaryotic cells. It was discovered by Italian biologist Camillo Golgi. The Golgi complex consists of a stack of flattened, membrane-bound sacs called cisternae, together with a system of associated vesicles known as Golgi vesicles. The cis face of Golgi complex is convex, while the trans face is concave and is called the maturing face, where the cisternae break up into vesicles. The most important function of the Golgi complex is the processing of cell secretions. These organelles are abundant in secretory cells. The cell secretions mainly consist of proteins.

The Golgi complex collects proteins from rough ER through smooth ER, modifies them to perform specific functions, and then exports these modified products in the form of vesicles. Certain organelles such as lysosomes, peroxisomes and glyoxysomes also originate from the Golgi complex. The Golgi complex is also involved in the formation of conjugated molecules like glycoproteins and lipoproteins. In plant cells during cell division, the Golgi complex gives rise to vesicles which contain cell wall synthesizing materials. At cytokinesis, these Golgi vesicles are arranged on the cell equator, fuse together and form a structure called phragmoplast. Later on, a new cell wall is derived from this structure. Lysosomes The word lyso means splitting and soma means body. Lysosomes are single membranous, spherical vesicles. They contain digestive or hydrolytic enzymes. The lysosomal enzymes are synthesized by the rough ER and then transported to the Golgi complex through smooth ER. After modification, these enzymes are released from the trans face of the Golgi complex in the form of vesicles. Such vesicles are called lysosomes. The newly formed lysosomes before the start of digestion are usually called primary lysosomes. In plants and protists, vacuoles carry out digestion, a function shared by lysosomes in animal cells. Lysosomes contain about 40 different digestive enzymes. These enzymes digest major macromolecules of the cell. The contents of lysosomes are acidic. During digestion, lysosomes fuse with membrane-bound vesicles formed by endocytosis, phagocytosis or autophagocytosis. These vesicles are referred to as endosomes, phagosomes and autophagosomes. After fusion with lysosomes, secondary lysosomes are formed. The biomolecules are broken down into smaller components like amino acids, monosaccharides, nucleotides and fatty acids which are then recycled in the cell. Functions of lysosomes include intracellular digestion, autophagy, autolysis and secretion of extracellular enzymes. The ingested food of the cell is stored in vesicles called food vacuoles. When a lysosome fuses with a food vacuole, the resulting structure is called secondary lysosome in which digestion begins. The digested products are absorbed by the cytoplasm while the remaining waste-containing vesicle is called residual body. Later on, residual bodies fuse with the cell membrane by exocytosis to eliminate undigested wastes. This process is known as intracellular digestion. Autophagy The process by which unwanted structures within the cell are engulfed and digested by lysosomes is called autophagy. It is a self-eating process of the cell in which lysosomes digest the cells own organelles. Such lysosomes are also called autophagosomes. Autophagy may occur during starvation to obtain energy or routinely to control the number of specific organelles. For example, when a person performs heavy muscular exercise, the number of mitochondria increases in muscle cells, but when exercise stops, excess mitochondria are removed by autophagy. Autolysis Autolysis occurs during developmental phases when a particular cell type is required to die. This type of cell death is programmed and is called autolysis. Due to this function, lysosomes are also called suicidal bags.

Lysosomal Storage Diseases If a particular lysosomal enzyme is absent or inactive, digestion of the corresponding substance is affected. As a result, the substance accumulates in the cell and causes serious problems. Such complications caused by the accumulation of substances due to the absence of certain lysosomal enzymes are called lysosomal storage diseases. These diseases are hereditary and congenital and therefore run in families. Most of these diseases are fatal in early childhood. More than 20 such diseases have been discovered so far. One common example is Tay-Sachs disease, in which a lipid-digesting enzyme is missing or inactive, resulting in accumulation of lipids in brain cells. Peroxisomes and Glyoxysomes Peroxisomes and glyoxysomes are collectively called microbodies. These are single membranous vesicular structures similar to lysosomes but smaller in size. They contain enzymes different from lysosomal enzymes and originate from the Golgi complex. Peroxisomes contain oxidative enzymes such as peroxidases, catalases and glycolic acid oxidase. They are abundant in liver cells and are involved in formation and decomposition of hydrogen peroxide. They are mainly concerned with detoxification of alcohol. In this process, alcohol is oxidized into hydrogen peroxide with the help of peroxidase enzyme. Hydrogen peroxide is toxic and is immediately broken down into water and oxygen by catalase enzyme. In plant cells, peroxisomes are involved in photorespiration. A step of photorespiration takes place in peroxisomes in which glycolate is converted into glycine. Glyoxysomes are found only at the seedling stage in oil seed plants. These organelles contain enzymes specific for plant lipid metabolism. Germinating seedlings convert stored fatty acids into carbohydrates through a metabolic pathway called glyoxylate cycle, the enzymes of which are present in glyoxysomes. Vacuoles Vacuoles are large vesicles originating from the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex and plasma membrane. Vacuoles perform a variety of functions in different kinds of cells. In animal cells, food vacuoles are formed by phagocytosis. Many freshwater protists possess contractile vacuoles that pump excess water out of the cell, thereby maintaining suitable concentration of ions and molecules inside the cell. In plant cells, vacuoles may also help in protection against herbivores by storing poisonous or unpleasant substances. Mature plant cells generally contain a single large central vacuole formed by the fusion of smaller vacuoles. The solution inside the vacuole, called cell sap, is the main reservoir of inorganic ions including chloride. The central vacuole plays a major role in mechanical support by maintaining turgor pressure and also acts as a storehouse of the cell. The membrane separating vacuole from cytoplasm is called tonoplast. Mitochondria Mitochondria (singular: mitochondrion) are present in all eukaryotic cells. Some cells possess a single large mitochondrion, but more often a cell has hundreds or thousands of mitochondria. The number of mitochondria correlates with the metabolic activity of the cell. Cells that move or contract have more mitochondria. Mitochondria are self-replicating and divide by fission. They are cylindrical or rod-shaped structures enclosed by a double membrane: outer membrane and inner membrane.

The outer membrane is smooth and freely permeable due to the presence of porins. The inner membrane is selectively permeable and folded inward to form cristae, which increase the surface area. The inner membrane divides the mitochondrion into two compartments: intermembrane space and mitochondrial matrix. The matrix contains enzymes, small circular DNA, RNA and ribosomes. These components indicate that mitochondria possess their own genetic system. Mitochondria are the sites of cellular respiration, the metabolic process that extracts energy from sugars, fats and other organic compounds. Enzymes of Krebs cycle are present in the mitochondrial matrix, while enzymes involved in electron transport chain and ATP synthesis are located on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Endosymbiotic Theory Mitochondria and chloroplasts show similarities with bacteria. Both are self-replicating, possess their own DNA and ribosomes (70S), and can survive outside the cell under laboratory conditions. These observations support the theory that mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living prokaryotic organisms that were engulfed by ancestral eukaryotic cells and formed a symbiotic relationship. Mitochondria are inherited maternally because they are present in the ovum but not in the sperm head. Plastids Plastids are found in plant and algal cells. They are essential for processes like photosynthesis and food storage. Based on pigment presence and stage of development, plastids are classified into proplastids, leucoplasts, chromoplasts and chloroplasts. Proplastids are immature plastids found in meristematic cells. They divide and differentiate into other types of plastids depending on conditions. Leucoplasts are colourless plastids found in roots, stems and seeds. They store food and are classified into amyloplasts, elaioplasts and proteinoplasts. Chromoplasts synthesize coloured pigments and are found in flowers and fruits where they help in pollination and seed dispersal. Chloroplasts are green plastids found in green parts of plants and are the sites of photosynthesis. Structure and Functions of Chloroplast Chloroplast is a discoid structure consisting of three parts: envelope, stroma and thylakoids. Each chloroplast is bounded by a double membrane called envelope. The outer membrane is freely permeable while the inner membrane is selectively permeable. Between them lies intermembrane space. Stroma is the colourless protein-rich matrix of chloroplast. It contains DNA, RNA, ribosomes and enzymes. Thylakoids are membrane-bound flattened sacs present in the stroma. Thylakoids are of two types: smaller thylakoids and larger thylakoids. Smaller thylakoids are stacked together to form grana. Each granum consists of 2550 thylakoids. Larger thylakoids connect grana and are called stroma lamellae. Photosynthetic pigments are present in the membranes of thylakoids. Chloroplast is the site of photosynthesis. Light-dependent reactions occur in the grana, while light-independent reactions occur in the stroma. Centrioles Centrioles are non-membranous organelles found mainly in animal cells. They are also present in some fungi and protists. Centrioles are cylindrical structures usually present in pairs at right angles near the nucleus. Each centriole is composed of nine triplets of microtubules arranged around a central axis. Before cell division, centrioles duplicate and migrate to opposite poles to form spindle fibres which help in chromosome separation.

Centrioles also give rise to basal bodies of cilia and flagella. Cytoskeleton Cytoskeleton consists of three types of fibrous structures: microfilaments, microtubules and intermediate filaments. Microfilaments are thin contractile fibres made of actin protein. They are involved in muscle contraction and relaxation. Microtubules are hollow cylindrical structures composed of tubulin protein. They play a role in spindle formation, cilia, flagella and centrioles. Intermediate filaments are thicker than microfilaments but thinner than microtubules. They provide mechanical support to the cell and maintain cell shape. Cilia and Flagella Cilia and flagella are hair-like projections on the surface of cells. They have the same internal structure but differ in length and number. Flagella are longer and fewer, while cilia are shorter and numerous. Both have a common ultrastructure consisting of a central pair of microtubules surrounded by nine pairs, forming a 92 arrangement. Cilia and flagella originate from basal bodies which have the same structure as centrioles. Movement of Cilia Movement of cilia occurs due to sliding of microtubule doublets. During effective stroke, cilium bends and moves fluid, while during recovery stroke it returns to original position. Movement of Flagella Flagellar movement occurs by propagation of waves from base to tip. This movement helps in locomotion, for example in human sperm cells. 3 Nucleus Nucleus is the largest and most important organelle of the cell. In animal cells it is centrally located, while in plant cells it is pushed to the side due to the presence of a large central vacuole. The eukaryotic nucleus consists of nuclear envelope, nucleoplasm, nucleolus and chromatin. Nuclear Envelope Nuclear envelope is a double membrane covering the nucleus. The two membranes are separated by perinuclear space. The outer membrane is continuous with endoplasmic reticulum and contains ribosomes. Nuclear pores are present in the nuclear envelope and are composed of transport proteins called nucleoporins. These pores regulate the exchange of materials between nucleus and cytoplasm. Nucleoplasm Nucleoplasm is the transparent fluid inside the nucleus containing proteins, enzymes, nucleotides and metal ions. It differs slightly from cytoplasm in composition. Nucleolus Nucleolus is a non-membranous structure present in nucleoplasm. It is involved in ribosome synthesis and contains rRNA and ribosomal subunits. Chromatin and Chromosomes Chromatin is a network of thin thread-like structures made of DNA and proteins. During cell division, chromatin condenses to form chromosomes. Each chromosome consists of two chromatids joined at centromere. The centromere contains kinetochore proteins which attach spindle fibres during cell division. Some chromosomes also possess secondary constrictions known as nucleolar organizers. 4 PROKARYOTIC AND EUKARYOTIC CELLS Two structurally different types of cells have evolved over time: prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. Prokaryotic cells include archaea, bacteria and cyanobacteria, while all other forms of life are composed of eukaryotic cells. Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound nucleus and organelles. Their DNA is dispersed in cytoplasm. Eukaryotic cells contain nucleus, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosomes, cytoskeleton and 80S ribosomes. Prokaryotic cells divide by binary fission, while eukaryotic cells divide by mitosis and meiosis.

DIGESTION INTRODUCTION You have read about biological molecules or food. Food is necessary for living beings. It is utilized at the cellular level. Most of the food we eat, however, is unavailable for utilization until it is mechanically and chemically reduced to forms that can cross the intestinal wall and transported to the cells by the blood. This chapter presents an overview of the digestive system, describes its anatomy, physiology and disorders of the digestive system and food habits. DIGESTIVE SYSTEM OF MAN The digestive system can be divided into two main groups: the gastrointestinal tract (GIT) and the accessory digestive organs. The organs of GIT are oral cavity, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine. The accessory organs are tongue, teeth, liver, gall bladder and pancreas. STRUCTURE The digestive tract, from the mouth to the anus, is a continuous tube that is modified at various points along its length, with each region performing a different role. GIT is approximately 9 m (30 ft) long. It passes through the abdominal cavity at the level of diaphragm. The digestive tube consists of four major layers: an internal mucosa and an external serosa, with submucosa and muscularis in between. These four layers are present in all parts of the digestive tube from the oesophagus to the anus. The mouth is surrounded by the cheeks, lips, tongue and a palate and forms a chamber between the palate and tongue called oral cavity. The tongue almost fills the oral cavity when the mouth is closed. Rough projections called papillae on the surface of the tongue cause friction, which is useful in manipulating the food. These papillae also contain taste buds. The palate forms the roof of the oral cavity. It consists of a hard anterior part the hard palate and a soft posterior part the soft palate. There are thirty two teeth. Different teeth are adapted to handle food in different ways. The incisors (front teeth) are chisel shaped and their sharp edges are used to bite off relatively large pieces of food. The canine teeth are cone shaped and they are useful in cutting or tearing or piercing food. The premolar and molars have broad surfaces and are adapted for grinding food particles. There are three pairs of salivary glands: parotid or parotis, submandibular and sublingual. These glands secrete saliva having only digestive enzymes. In the oral cavity both mechanical and chemical digestion takes place. Mechanical digestion involves chewing food into smaller masses while chemical digestion involves enzymatic breakdown of food. MASTICATION: Thorough chewing of food breaks the connective tissue covering and increases the exposed surface area of the food particles for the action of digestive enzymes. Food taken into the mouth is chewed, or masticated, by the teeth. Mastication breaks large pieces into smaller ones, which have a larger total surface area for the action of digestive enzymes. It also increases the surface area for the digestive enzymes. INFLAMMATION OF PAROTID GLAND: Inflammation of parotid gland is called parotiditis or parotitis.

The most common type of parotiditis is caused by a viral infection called mumps. SALIVA SECRETION: Saliva is secreted by salivary glands. The watery part of saliva contains an enzyme called salivary amylase, which digests starch. Mucin is a proteoglycan that gives a lubricating quality to the secretions of the salivary glands. Saliva moistens food and mucous membrane. Saliva contains various mineral salts including chloride ions which speed up the activity of enzymes. Saliva prevents bacterial infection in the mouth as it contains lysozyme and immunoglobulin. Saliva has a pH between 6.00 and 7.0, a favourable range for the digestive action of amylase. PHARYNX: The pharynx is a cavity behind the mouth. The tongue forms the chewed and moistened food into a ball like mass called bolus and pushes it into the pharynx. Muscles raise the soft palate against the back wall of the pharynx, which closes the passage between nasal cavity and pharynx, preventing food from entering the nasal cavity. The pressure of the food in the pharynx stimulates nerves in its walls and initiates the swallowing reflex, an involuntary action. As part of this reflex action the voice box larynx rises up to meet the epiglottis, with this action epiglottis cartilage drops over the opening to the larynx and trachea. In this way food is passed over the trachea without entering it. After food enters the oesophagus, the soft palate lowers and the epiglottis is raised. OESOPHAGUS: The oesophagus is that part of the digestive tube that extends between the pharynx and the stomach. It is about 25 cm long. It begins at the base of the pharynx and descends behind the trachea. The oesophagus penetrates the diaphragm and is continuous with the stomach. Function: Digestion which started in the oral cavity continues in the oesophagus. As oesophagus is a passage way so no digestion takes place here. PERISTALSIS: The movement of food is followed by relaxation of the tube wall and the contraction of circular muscles behind the bolus. The wave of relaxation of the tube wall followed by the wave of contraction of circular muscles that propels the mass of the bolus forward along the digestive tract. As the food enters and expands the tube wall, the pressure stimulates peristalsis. Sometimes, the direction of peristalsis become opposite in direction, and is called antiperistalsis that leads to vomiting. STOMACH The stomach is an enlarged segment of the digestive tract in the left superior part of the abdomen immediately below the diaphragm. When empty, the stomach is continuous with the oesophagus at the cardiac opening (located near the heart). The stomach consists of three major regions: the cardiac region, the body, and the pyloric region. A cross section of the stomach wall illustrates its histology, including several gastric pits and glands. The serosa is the outer most layer of the stomach. The muscularis of the stomach consists of three layers: an outer longitudinal layer, a middle circular layer and an inner oblique layer.

The next two layers are submucosa and mucosa. The stomach is lined with simple columnar epithelium. The mucosal surface forms numerous tube like gastric pits, which are openings for the gastric glands. The epithelial cells of stomach can be divided into four general types. The first type is surface mucous cells, which produce mucus, is on the surface and within the gastric pit. The remaining three are in the gastric gland. They are: (1) Parietal (Oxyntic) cells produce hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factors (2) Chief (Zymogenic) cells produce pepsinogen (3) Endocrine cells secrete the hormone gastrin into the blood. FUNCTIONS OF STOMACH Digestion in the stomach can be divided into two types: mechanical digestion and chemical digestion. Mechanical Digestion: The mixing action of the stomach walls allows mechanical digestion in the stomach. The smooth muscles of the stomach produce contractions called mixing waves. This is made more efficient by the fact that unlike other region of the digestive tract, stomach has three layers of smooth muscles. The churning action of the stomach helps to mix the boluses of food with gastric juice. This mixing leads to the production of a thick liquid known as chyme. Gastric Juice: Stomach secretions include mucus, hydrochloric acid, pepsinogen. The mucous cells secrete viscous and alkaline mucus. This mucus protects the epithelial cells of the stomach wall against the damaging effect of acidic gastric juice. Hydrochloric acid produces the low pH of the stomach, which is normally close to 2. Although the hydrochloric acid exerted has a minor digestive effect on digested food, one of its main functions is to kill bacteria that are ingested with essentially everything humans put into their mouths. The low pH also stops carbohydrate digestion by inactivating salivary amylase. The low pH denatures many proteins so that proteolytic enzymes can reach internal peptide bonds. It also provides the proper pH environment for the function of pepsin. Chief cells within the gastric glands secrete inactive pepsinogen. Pepsinogen is stored in zymogen granules, which are released by exocytosis when pepsinogen secretion is stimulated. Once pepsinogen enters the lumen of the stomach, it is converted to pepsin by hydrochloric acid and previously formed pepsin molecules. Pepsin exhibits optimum enzymatic activity at a pH of 3 or less. Pepsin catalyzes the cleavage of some covalent bonds in proteins, breaking them into smaller peptide chains. Role of nervous system and gastrin hormone on the secretion of gastric juice: Approximately 2-3 litres of gastric juice are produced each day. Both nervous and hormonal mechanisms regulate gastric secretions. Hormones that regulate stomach secretions include gastrin, secretin, gastric inhibitory polypeptide, and cholecystokinin. The sensations of the taste and smell of food, stimulation of tactile receptors during the process of chewing and swallowing, and pleasant thoughts of food stimulate centres within the medulla that influences gastric secretion.

Neuronal stimulation of the stomach mucosa results in the secretion of acetylcholine, which stimulates the secretory activity of both the parietal and chief cells and stimulates the secretion of gastrin from endocrine cells. Gastrin is released into the circulation and travels to the parietal cells, where it stimulates additional hydrochloric acid secretion. The greatest volume of gastric secretions is initiated by the presence of food in the stomach. The primary stimuli are distention of the stomach and the presence of amino acids and peptides in the stomach. Peristaltic waves occur less frequently, are significantly more forceful than mixing waves, and force the chyme near the periphery of the stomach toward the pyloric sphincter. The pyloric sphincter usually remains partially closed because of mild tonic contraction. Each peristaltic contraction is sufficiently strong to force a small amount of chyme through the pyloric opening and into the duodenum. SMALL INTESTINE Small intestine consists of three parts: the duodenum, the jejunum and the ileum. It is about 6 m long. DUODENUM: Duodenum is the first part of small intestine. It is about 25 cm in length. Here food from the stomach mixes with secretions from the pancreas and the liver. The most important enzymes are (a) Pancreatic amylase: It hydrolyses the polysaccharides into maltose. It is the most powerful starch digesting enzyme. It hydrolyses starch to maltose. (b) Pancreatic lipase: It is the principal enzyme for the hydrolysis of fats (triglycerides). It hydrolyses fats into monoglycerides, diglycerides, glycerol and fatty acids. (c) Proteases: Important enzyme precursors are found in pancreatic juice. They are trypsinogen and chymotrypsinogen. Both are the inactive forms. The intestinal glands secrete an activator enzyme called enterokinase. The enterokinase converts trypsinogen into trypsin. Trypsin then activates more trypsinogen. The active trypsin then activates more trypsinogen. The active trypsin then activates chymotrypsinogen into its active digestive form, which acts on proteins and converts them into polypeptides. BILE: Bile is manufactured in liver but stored in gall bladder. Bile contains no digestive enzymes. Bile emulsifies fat causing large globules to break into numerous small droplets called micelles. Emulsification provides relatively large surface area of lipid for the action of lipase enzyme and speed up the digestion of fats and oils. JEJUNUM AND ILEUM: Jejunum is about 2.5 m long and ileum is about 3.5 m long. Here the digestion of proteins, carbohydrates and fats is completed. The lining of the jejunum and ileum secrete several enzymes: Erepsin: It splits peptides into amino acids. Lactase: It converts lactose to glucose and galactose. Maltase: It converts maltose to glucose. Sucrase: it converts sucrose to glucose and fructose. Pancreatic lipase: It completes the digestion of fats into fatty acids and glycerol. By the action of these enzymes, chyme is turned into a watery emulsion called chyle. ABSORPTION OF DIGESTED FOOD FROM THE LUMEN OF INTESTINE Small intestine is the major site of nutrient absorption. Tiny finger like projections of the mucosa called villi, which are 0.5-1.5 mm in length.

Each villus is covered by simple columnar epithelium and contains a blood capillary network and a lymph capillary called lacteal. Villi greatly increase the surface area of small intestine and make it more efficient. Intestinal walls are folded to increase surface area. ABSORPTION OF CARBOHYDRATES: Absorption occurs by a combination of simple diffusion and active transport. The monosaccharides are transferred by facilitated diffusion to the blood capillaries of intestinal villi and are carried by the hepatic portal system to the liver, where non-glucose sugars are converted to glucose. Glucose enters the capillaries through facilitated diffusion. ABSORPTION OF LIPIDS: Lipids digest into fatty acids and glycerol. Glycerol and fatty acid are absorbed by epithelial cells. They are recombined into fats within the epithelial cells. They are then mixed with cholesterol and phospholipids forming small globules called chylomicrons, most of which are transported by exocytosis from the basal surface of epithelial cells into lacteals. Lymph containing chylomicrons eventually drains from the lymphatic system into the blood. ABSORPTION OF PROTEINS: Proteins are absorbed in epithelial cells of villi by active transport and carried by blood capillaries to liver and then to body cells. Amino acids are used for making new proteins, but some amino acids may be used for energy production. LARGE INTESTINE The junction between ileum and large intestine is ileocecal junction guarded by ileocecal valve. The caecum, which is the proximal end of the large intestine, is where the large and small intestine meet. Attached to the caecum is a small blind tube about 9 cm long called vermiform appendix. The walls of the appendix contain many lymph nodules. The colon is about 1.5 m long and consists of four parts: the ascending colon, transverse colon, descending colon, and sigmoid colon. The rectum is a straight, muscular tube that begins at the termination of the sigmoid colon and ends at the anus guarded by sphincter. FUNCTIONS OF LARGE INTESTINE: The large intestine performs several important functions. The major functions of the large intestine are: (a) Absorbing water and electrolytes (b) Absorption of vitamins (c) Neutralizing acidity and protecting from infections. Absorbing water and electrolytes: Further digestion or breaking down of nutrients does not take place in the large intestine. The proximal half of the large intestine functions to reabsorb most of the water and electrolytes making the stools solid. The substances that remain in the lumen becomes faeces, which is stored for a time in the distal portion of the large intestine. Absorption of vitamins: The large intestine also helps in absorption of vitamins made by bacteria that normally live in the large intestine. These bacteria also produce large amounts of vitamins. The most important of these is Vitamin K and Biotin (a B vitamin). Neutralizing acidity and protecting from infections: The mucosa of the large intestine also: (a) secretes bicarbonates to neutralize the increased acidity resulting from the formation of fatty acids and other digestive components at earlier parts of the intestines.

(b) Acts as a barrier and protect from microbial infections and invasions. DEFECATION: When appropriate, a person usually can initiate the defecation reflex (also called bowel movement) by holding a deep breath and contracting the abdominal muscles. This increases the internal pressure and forces the faeces into the rectum. When the rectum is filled, its wall is distended and the defecation reflex is triggered. A wave of peristalsis in the descending colon is stimulated, and the internal and external anal sphincter is signalled to relax and the faeces are expelled. The reflex persists only for a few minutes and quickly dies. A person can inhibit defecation by keeping the external sphincter contracted. ACCESSORY ORGANS: Accessory organs of the digestive system are liver, gall bladder and pancreas. LIVER: Liver is the largest internal organ of the body. The liver consists of two major lobes and two minor lobes. Secretion of bile: The liver produces and secretes bile. It is stored in the gall bladder. Bile contains no digestive enzymes. Bile consists of water, bile salts sodium glycocholate and sodium taurocholate, bile pigment bilirubin, cholesterols, lecithin (a phospholipid) mucus, cells and salts. Role of constituents of bile: Bile salts reduce the surface tension of fat globules and emulsify them into droplets and thus increase their total surface area. This process is called emulsification. These small droplets are then acted upon by lipase enzyme. Bilirubin results from the breakdown of hemoglobin. In the intestine, bacteria convert bilirubin to pigments that give the faeces its characteristic brown colour. Some of these pigments are absorbed from the intestine, modified in the kidneys and excreted in the urine, contributing to the characteristic yellowish colour of the urine. Bile salts help in the absorption of fatty acids from the intestinal tract. Secretion of bile is related to secretin hormone: Fatty acids in the lumen of the duodenum stimulate endocrine cells to release the hormone cholecystokinin (CCK). CCK stimulates contractions in the smooth muscle of the gall bladder allowing bile release into the duodenum. Acidic chyme in the lumen of the duodenum stimulates other endocrine cells to release the hormone secretin. Secretin produced by the duodenum is carried through the circulatory system to the liver and stimulates liver to release bicarbonate into the bile. FUNCTIONS OF LIVER: The liver performs important digestive and excretory functions, stores and processes nutrients, synthesizes new molecules and detoxifies harmful chemicals. Storage role of liver: Hepatocytes can remove sugar from the blood and store it in the form of glycogen. They can also store fat, vitamins (A, B12, D, E, and K), copper and iron. This storage is usually short-term and the amount of stored material in the hepatocytes varies and liver size fluctuates during a given day. Metabolic role of liver: The metabolism of glucose occurs in liver. Whenever needed, it breaks glycogen into glucose (glycogenolysis). Glucose is also synthesized from non-carbohydrates (gluconeogenesis). Deamination of amino acids also occurs in liver cells. Excess of amino acids is deaminated.

Deamination of amino acids produces keto acids and ammonia. Ammonia produced by deamination of amino acids is converted into urea (ornithine-arginine cycle). Synthesis of vitamin A from carotene and synthesis of albumin from amino acids takes place in liver. Many of the blood proteins (like prothrombin, fibrinogen) are synthesized in liver which are necessary for blood clotting. Phagocytosis also occurs in liver i.e., dead erythrocytes are destroyed. The bile pigments bilirubin (orange pigment) and biliverdin (green pigment) are formed from the breakdown of haemoglobin. Liver produces heparin, an anticoagulant that prevents clotting of blood inside the blood vessels. Red blood cells are formed in foetal life. Detoxification occurs in liver. GALL BLADDER: The gall bladder is a saclike structure on the inferior surface of the liver that is about 8 cm long and 4 cm wide. The gall bladder is connected to the common bile duct by the cystic duct. Bile is continually secreted by the liver. PANCREAS: Pancreas is a complex organ composed of both endocrine and exocrine tissues. It is located posterior to the spleen. The endocrine portion produces the hormones insulin and glucagon. The exocrine portion produces pancreatic juice. COMPOSITION OF PANCREATIC JUICE: Pancreatic juice consists of an aqueous bicarbonate component and an enzymatic component. Bicarbonate neutralizes the acidic chyme entering the small intestine from the stomach. The enzymatic component contains enzymes important for the digestion of all major classes of food. The major proteolytic enzymes are trypsin, chymotrypsin, and carboxypeptidase. These are secreted in their inactive forms as trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, and procarboxypeptidase and are activated by the removal of certain peptides from the larger precursor proteins. If these were produced in their active forms, they would digest the tissues that produce them. Trypsinogen is activated by the proteolytic enzyme enterokinase into trypsin. Trypsin then activates more trypsinogen, as well as chymotrypsinogen and procarboxypeptidase. Amylase continues the polysaccharide digestion that was initiated in the oral cavity. Pancreatic lipases breakdown lipids into free fatty acids, glycerides, and cholesterol. Deoxyribonucleases and ribonucleases reduce DNA and ribonucleic acid to their component nucleotides, respectively. SECRETION OF PANCREATIC JUICE AND SECRETIN HORMONE: Pancreatic juice secretion is regulated by the hormones secretin and cholecystokinin which are produced by the walls of the duodenum upon detection of acid food, proteins, fats and vitamins. Pancreatic secretion consists of an aqueous bicarbonate component from the duct cells and enzymatic component from the acinar cells. A clear alkaline secretion of the pancreas containing enzymes that aid in the digestion of proteins, carbohydrates, and fats. The predominant effect of secretin on the pancreas is to stimulate duct cells to secrete water and bicarbonate. As soon as this occurs, the enzymes secreted by the acinar cells are flushed out of the pancreas, through the pancreatic duct into the duodenum. DISORDERS OF DIGESTIVE SYSTEM: Here we will describe causes, prevention and treatment of the disorders related to digestive system and food habits: ulcer, food poisoning, dyspepsia, obesity, anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa.

PEPTIC ULCER: Peptic ulcer is classically viewed as a condition in which the stomach acids damage the mucosal lining of the GI tract itself. Helicobacter pylori is the most important factor in ulcer development, accounting for 90 of duodenal ulcer and 70 of the gastric ulcer. Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents are an important cause of peptic ulcer. Peptic ulcer tends to run in families i.e., it is a hereditary disease. Other risk factors such as smoking, aspirin, excess intake of coffee should be avoided. Treatment: Mainstay of treatment are antacid like milk, anticholinergic drugs, drugs which reduce acid production such as Cimetidine, antibiotics to kill bacteria. FOOD POISONING: It includes diarrhoea, vomiting and abdominal pain. It is an illness from ingestion of food containing toxic substances. Aetiology: Due to the toxins produced by bacteria, Salmonella and Campylobacter. Prevention: Basic hygiene should be followed. Avoid unboiled / unbottled water, ice, cubes, salads and peel on fruits. Consume freshly prepared hot food or thoroughly rewarmed food. Treatment: Soft easily digested diet, such as soup, fruits drinks, tea and cold drinks are preferred. Oral rehydration salt (ORS) is given. Antidiarrhoeal agent such as Loperamide, antibiotics are prescribed. DYSPEPSIA: Incomplete or imperfect digestion is called dyspepsia. Aetiology: It may occur due to excessive acidity in stomach or faulty function of stomach and intestine or insufficient quality and quantity of bile secretion. Prevention: Avoid food that worsens symptoms. Stop smoking, weight reduction, small meals, avoid alcohol, tea, fatty food, heavy lifting, bending specially after meals and late night meals to avoid acid reflex during sleep. Treatment: Antibiotics to be given against this disease. Drugs which decrease acid production such as Cimetidine; stop NSAID (Non-Steroidal Anti inflammatory Drugs); use antacids. OBESITY: When a person has an abnormal amount of fat on the body it is called obesity. BULIMIA NERVOSA: It is a neurotic disorder in slightly older girls. It is characterized by bouts of overeating of fattening food such as fried food or cream cakes. This voracious overeating is followed immediately by self-induced vomiting, fasting or purging (to empty bowel). This may cause physical effects including serum electrolytes imbalance and frequent vomiting infections. Treatment: Treatment of bulimics is likely to be prolonged. The initial treatment is to overcome the effects of weight loss and malnutrition. It is necessary to undertake the treatment in hospital under strict supervision. ANOREXIA NERVOSA: It is the loss of appetite due to the fear of becoming obese. Such a feeling is common in young females between the ages of 12 and 21 years. Usually just after the onset of puberty. Symptoms: It includes loss of appetite due to the fear of becoming obese. The anorexic girl over estimates the size of her own body and so insists that she is overweight, when in reality her weight has dropped to a dangerous level. These girls are often not matured psychologically and unable to cope with the challenges of puberty and their emerging sexuality.

The losses of feminine characteristics enable the girls to retreat into a childlike state in which she feels safe. Therapy: Psychiatric therapy is usually required to treat anorexic girls. Such patients are fed through any other route other than alimentary canal, i.e., intravenously. The recovery is usually slow over 2-4 years and in some cases longer. Science Technology and Society Connections: Relate food poisoning and dyspepsia with eating habits of the society.
